arXiv:1702.05715v2 [gr-qc] 22 Feb 2019

Strong cosmic censorship in spherical symmetry for two-ended asymptotically flat initial data I. The interior of the black hole region

Jonathan Luk Address: Department of Mathematics, Stanford University, Palo Alto, CA, USA Email address: jluk@stanford.edu and Sung-Jin Oh Address: Korea Institute for Advanced Study, Seoul, Korea Email address: sjoh@kias.re.kr
Abstract.

This is the first and main paper of a two-part series, in which we prove the C2C^{2}-formulation of the strong cosmic censorship conjecture for the Einstein–Maxwell–(real)–scalar–field system in spherical symmetry for two-ended asymptotically flat data. For this model, it is known through the works of Dafermos and Dafermos–Rodnianski that the maximal globally hyperbolic future development of any admissible two-ended asymptotically flat Cauchy initial data set possesses a non-empty Cauchy horizon, across which the spacetime is C0C^{0}-future-extendible (in particular, the C0C^{0}-formulation of the strong cosmic censorship conjecture is false). Nevertheless, the main conclusion of the present series of papers is that for a generic (in the sense of being open and dense relative to appropriate topologies) class of such data, the spacetime is future-inextendible with a Lorentzian metric of higher regularity (specifically, C2C^{2}).

In this paper, we prove that the solution is C2C^{2}-future-inextendible under the condition that the scalar field obeys an L2L^{2}-averaged polynomial lower bound along each of the event horizons. This, in particular, improves upon a previous result of Dafermos, which required instead a pointwise lower bound. Key to the proof are appropriate stability and instability results in the interior of the black hole region, whose proofs are in turn based on ideas from the work of Dafermos–Luk on the stability of the Kerr Cauchy horizon (without symmetry) and from our previous paper on linear instability of Reissner–Nordström Cauchy horizon. In the second paper of the series [36], which concerns analysis in the exterior of the black hole region, we show that the L2L^{2}-averaged polynomial lower bound needed for the instability result indeed holds for a generic class of admissible two-ended asymptotically flat Cauchy initial data.

1. Introduction

This is the first of a series of two papers in which we prove the C2C^{2}-formulation of the strong cosmic censorship conjecture for the Einstein–Maxwell–(real)–scalar–field system in spherical symmetry for two-ended asymptotically flat initial data on ℝ×𝕊2\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{S}^{2}. A solution to the Einstein–Maxwell–(real)–scalar–field system consists of (ℳ,g,ϕ,F)(\mathcal{M},g,\phi,F), where ℳ\mathcal{M} is a 44-dimensional manifold, gg is a Lorentzian metric on ℳ\mathcal{M}, ϕ\phi is a real-valued function on ℳ\mathcal{M} and FF is a 22-form on ℳ\mathcal{M}. The system of equations is given by

{R​i​cμ​ν−12​gμ​ν​R=2​(Tμ​ν(s​f)+Tμ​ν(e​m)),Tμ​ν(s​f)=∂μϕ​∂νϕ−12​gμ​ν​(g−1)α​β​∂αϕ​∂βϕ,Tμ​ν(e​m)=(g−1)α​β​Fμ​α​Fν​β−14​gμ​ν​(g−1)α​β​(g−1)γ​σ​Fα​γ​Fβ​σ,\begin{cases}Ric_{\mu\nu}-\frac{1}{2}g_{\mu\nu}R=2(T^{(sf)}_{\mu\nu}+T^{(em)}_{\mu\nu}),\\ T^{(sf)}_{\mu\nu}=\partial_{\mu}\phi\partial_{\nu}\phi-\frac{1}{2}g_{\mu\nu}(g^{-1})^{\alpha\beta}\partial_{\alpha}\phi\partial_{\beta}\phi,\\ T^{(em)}_{\mu\nu}=(g^{-1})^{\alpha\beta}F_{\mu\alpha}F_{\nu\beta}-\frac{1}{4}g_{\mu\nu}(g^{-1})^{\alpha\beta}(g^{-1})^{\gamma\sigma}F_{\alpha\gamma}F_{\beta\sigma},\end{cases} (1.1)

where ϕ\phi and FF satisfy

□g​ϕ=0,d​F=0,(g−1)α​μ​∇αFμ​ν=0.\Box_{g}\phi=0,\,\quad dF=0,\,\quad(g^{-1})^{\alpha\mu}\nabla_{\alpha}F_{\mu\nu}=0.

Here, □g\Box_{g} and ∇\nabla respectively denote the Laplace–Beltrami operator and the Levi–Civita connection associated to the metric gg.

An explicit spherically symmetric solution to this system with a vanishing scalar field is the Reissner--Nordström spacetime, whose metric is given in local coordinates by11 1 We will use boldface 𝐞{\bf e} for the charge in this paper and reserve the notation ee for the Euler number.

g=−(1−2​Mr+𝐞2r2)​d​t2+(1−2​Mr+𝐞2r2)−1​d​r2+r2​d​σ𝕊2,g=-\left(1-\frac{2M}{r}+\frac{{\bf e}^{2}}{r^{2}}\right)dt^{2}+\left(1-\frac{2M}{r}+\frac{{\bf e}^{2}}{r^{2}}\right)^{-1}dr^{2}+r^{2}d\sigma_{\mathbb{S}^{2}}, (1.2)

where d​σ𝕊2d\sigma_{\mathbb{S}^{2}} denotes the standard round metric on the 22-sphere with radius 11 and the Maxwell field FF is given by22 2 We remark on the well-known fact that there are different choices of (spherically symmetric) Maxwell field which together with the metric (1.2) solve the Einstein–Maxwell equations. Here, we are only giving one such example. F=2​𝐞r2​d​t∧d​rF=\frac{2{\bf e}}{r^{2}}\,dt\wedge dr. Here, MM and 𝐞{\bf e} are real-valued constants representing the mass and the charge of the spacetime respectively.

The Reissner–Nordström spacetime is said to be subextremal with non-vanishing charge if 0<|𝐞|<M0<|{\bf e}|<M. In this case, the maximal globally hyperbolic future development of Reissner--Nordström initial data has a Penrose diagram33 3 In this work, we make an extensive use of Penrose diagrams to represent global causal properties of the spacetime. For an introduction, see [18, Appendix C]. given by Figure 1. In particular, the spacetime possesses a smooth Cauchy horizon 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+} and the maximal globally hyperbolic future development can be future-extended smoothly but non-uniquely as solutions to the Einstein–Maxwell system.

A priori, the non-uniqueness of possible future-extensions of the Reissner–Nordström spacetime challenges the deterministic nature of Einstein’s theory. Nevertheless, it is widely expected that such a feature of the Reissner–Nordström spacetime is non-generic. This non-genericity, understood from the point of view of the initial value problem, would follow from the celebrated strong cosmic censorship of Penrose [44]. Since we will be dealing with the Einstein--Maxwell--scalar field system in this paper, we state the strong cosmic censorship conjecture in the following form44 4 One can of course also entertain the strong cosmic censorship conjecture for the Einstein–Maxwell system or the Einstein vacuum system. The conjecture can also be formulated in situations where the initial data are not asymptotically flat, for instance in cosmological settings; see for instance [47]. We will not discuss the conjecture in such generality in this paper.:

Conjecture 1.1 (Strong cosmic censorship conjecture).

Maximal globally hyperbolic future developments for the Einstein–Maxwell–(real)–scalar field system to generic asymptotically flat initial data are future-inextendible as suitably regular Lorentzian manifolds.

The strong cosmic censorship conjecture as stated above is not precise regarding the notion of regularity for the extension. One may entertain the following slightly more precise formulation of the conjecture:

Conjecture 1.2 (CkC^{k}-formulation of the strong cosmic censorship conjecture).

Maximal globally hyperbolic future developments for the Einstein–Maxwell–(real)–scalar field system corresponding to generic asymptotically flat initial data are future-inextendible as time-oriented Lorentzian manifolds with CkC^{k} metrics.

Our purpose in this paper and [36] is to understand Conjecture 1.2 for generic spherically symmetric solutions. However, when discussing the strong cosmic censorship conjecture under the assumption of spherical symmetry, one should be reminded that the set of spherically symmetric solutions is only a very small subset of solutions and their behavior may not be representative of the “generic” phenomena in general without symmetry assumptions. Nevertheless, in view of [16], we hope that some of the methods we develop in this paper may be relevant for Conjecture 1.2 in some settings without symmetry assumptions.

In view of the fact that the explicit Schwarzschild solution is inextendible to a larger Lorentzian manifold with a continuous metric [49], one may conjecture a very strong form of the strong cosmic censorship conjecture, namely, the C0C^{0}-formulation of Conjecture 1.2 [8]. This would be consistent with the expectation, which is common in the physics literature, that the “tidal deformation becomes infinite” in the interior of black holes. Indeed, for spherically symmetric solutions such that in addition the Maxwell field is assumed to vanish, i.e., for solutions to the Einstein–(real)–scalar field system in spherical symmetry, the C0C^{0}-formulation of the strong cosmic censorship conjecture was proven by Christodoulou:

Theorem 1.3 (Christodoulou [6, 7]).

The C0C^{0}-formulation of the strong cosmic censorship conjecture for the Einstein–(real)–scalar field system in spherical symmetry with either 11-ended asymptotically flat initial data on ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} or 22-ended asymptotically flat initial data on ℝ×𝕊2\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{S}^{2} is true.

Nevertheless, Dafermos--Rodnianski showed that as long as the charge is non-zero55 5 As we will see in Section 2, the charge is a constant for solutions to the Einstein–Maxwell–(real)–scalar field system in spherical symmetry. It therefore makes sense to discuss solutions with non-vanishing charge.66 6 Notice that the Schwarzschild solution is not a solution to the Einstein–Maxwell–(real)–scalar field system in the case where the charge is required to be non-vanishing., all solutions arising from a suitable class of initial data are extendible with a C0C^{0} metric. Hence, if one views the non-vanishing of charge as a “generic” condition, this implies that the C0C^{0}-formulation of strong cosmic censorship is false for the Einstein–Maxwell–(real)–scalar field system in spherical symmetry:

Theorem 1.4 (Dafermos [14], Dafermos–Rodnianski [18]).

The C0C^{0}-formulation of the strong cosmic censorship conjecture for the Einstein–Maxwell–(real)–scalar field system in spherical symmetry with 22-ended asymptotically flat initial data on ℝ×𝕊2\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{S}^{2} is false.

Our main result in this series of papers is that the C2C^{2}-formulation of the strong cosmic censorship conjecture remains true in this setting:

Theorem 1.5 (Main theorem, rough version).

The C2C^{2}-formulation of the strong cosmic censorship conjecture for the Einstein–Maxwell–(real)–scalar field system in spherical symmetry with 22-ended asymptotically flat initial data on ℝ×𝕊2\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{S}^{2} is true.

In view of the above discussion, one only needs to understand the case where the charge is non-vanishing. We will make this assumption from now on.

Remark 1.6 (Wl​o​c1,2W^{1,2}_{loc} formulation of the strong cosmic censorship).

Theorems 1.4 and 1.5 leave open the question of the validity of some “intermediate” formulation of the strong cosmic censorship conjecture (for instance, the C1C^{1} formulation of the strong cosmic censorship). At the same time, it is also of interest to consider a formulation of the strong cosmic censorship not in the class of CkC^{k} metrics, but in terms of Wl​o​c1,2W^{1,2}_{loc} metrics. This is particularly relevant to the problem of determinism since C0∩Wl​o​c1,2C^{0}\cap W^{1,2}_{loc} is the minimal known requirement to define weak solutions to the Einstein–Maxwell–(real)–scalar–field system; see the discussions in the introduction of [9].

In support of the Wl​o​c1,2W^{1,2}_{loc} formulation of the conjecture, we show in Appendix C that in a particular C0C^{0} extension of a generic solution whose existence is asserted by Theorem 1.4 (more precisely, see Theorems 5.1 and 5.5 below), the Christoffel symbols, as well as the gradient of the scalar field, fail to be locally square-integrable77 7 In fact, we prove a stronger blow up result for the Christoffel symbols in this extension, namely that they are not in Ll​o​cpL^{p}_{loc} for all p>1p>1, while for the gradient of the scalar field we only show the failure of the Ll​o​c2L^{2}_{loc} condition.. The Wl​o​c1,2W^{1,2}_{loc} formulation of the strong cosmic censorship conjecture would follow if such blow up statements may be generalized to arbitrary nontrivial C0C^{0} extensions. We do not pursue this issue in this paper, which remains an open problem.

We will give a precise statement of Theorem 1.5 in Section 3. In particular, we will define the notion of genericity, which very roughly is to be understood as being open in a (weighted) C1C^{1} topology and being dense88 8 In fact, a stronger statement is proven: for any element in the complement of the generic set, there exists a continuous (with respect to a weighted-C∞C^{\infty}-topology) 11-parameter family of initial data sets passing through it such that all other elements of the 11-parameter family belong to the generic set. in a (weighted) C∞C^{\infty} topology. The theorem will then be proven in Section 7, using some results that are proven in the later parts of the paper, as well as some results which are proven in the companion paper [36]. We refer the reader to Section 1.1 below for the main elements of the proof. Theorem 1.5 in particular implies that the smooth Cauchy horizon of Reissner–Nordström is unstable. In the special case of small perturbations of Reissner–Nordström, we in fact have more precise information regarding the maximal globally hyperbolic development, see Section 3.6.

Prior to the present paper, the best known result regarding the validity of the C2C^{2}-formulation of the strong cosmic censorship for this model in spherical symmetry was achieved in the seminal work of Dafermos [14] (see also [12, 15]), who proved a conditional C2C^{2}-future-inextendibility result99 9 In [14], C1C^{1}-future-inextendibility within spherical symmetry was proven, but C2C^{2}-future-inextendibility without symmetry was not explicitly shown. This however follows easily from the mass inflation result.. The required condition, however, remains difficult to verify1010 10 In fact, it is not known whether there exists a single regular solution such that this condition is satisfied.. Part of our proof is to obtain a new and stronger conditional inextendibility result, so that we show moreover that the condition is satisfied for a generic set of data. See Section 1.2.4 for further discussions.

We remark at this point that the class of 22-ended initial data that we consider in this paper and [36] can be easily shown to have a complete future null infinity (with two connected components) [13]. Indeed, this is the main simplification that arises from studying the 22-ended case so that we in particular do not need to handle potential singularities at the center of symmetry. For a more ‘‘realistic’’ model1111 11 Notice that there are no regular 11-ended solutions to the Einstein–Maxwell–(real)–scalar field system with data on ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} in the presence of charge., one may for instance study the Einstein–Maxwell–(charged)–scalar–field system with spherically symmetric initial data posed on ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}, for which the strong cosmic censorship conjecture remains an open problem. In that case, the full resolution of the strong cosmic censorship conjecture seems to at least require an understanding of singularities arising at the centers of symmetry as well as Cauchy horizons emanating from them [35].

The remainder of the introduction will be structured as follows:

  • •

    In Section 1.1, we explain the overall structure of the proof of Theorem 1.5. The reader is encouraged to take this as a guide to our series of papers.

  • •

    In Section 1.2, we give a brief overview of some of the relevant previous results. In particular, we provide comparison of our proof with that of linear instability of Reissner–Nordström Cauchy horizon in [38], and with the possible alternative approach using the conditional instability theorem of Dafermos [14].

  • •

    Finally, we end the introduction with an outline of the remainder of the paper in Section 1.3.

1.1. Guide to the series: Structure of the proof of Theorem 1.5

In very rough terms, the proof of Theorem 1.5 proceeds by first showing that the maximal globally hyperbolic future developments of any “admissible” data approach Reissner–Nordström in a certain sense, and then using the ideas in [38] (which were originally for linear instability on fixed Reissner–Nordström; see Section 1.2 below) to prove nonlinear instability of the Cauchy horizon in the near-Reissner–Nordström region in the “generic” case. Finally, we use nonlinear methods specific to the Einstein–Maxwell–(real)–scalar–field system in spherical symmetry to derive the desired global C2C^{2}-future-inextendibility property from the aforementioned nonlinear instability.

To discuss the main result and its proof in more detail, we begin with a brief description of the notions of “admissible” and “generic” initial data, which are necessary for a precise formulation of the strong cosmic censorship conjecture.

Definition of admissible initial data and genericity (Definitions 3.1 and 3.5). Roughly speaking, we will consider admissible Cauchy initial data sets which consists of data for the geometric quantities and the matter fields, which are spherically symmetric, two-ended asymptotically flat, future admissible, and have non-vanishing charge. Some remarks on these aspects are in order.

  • •

    By asymptotically flat, we mean that the data for the metric, the Maxwell field and the scalar field approach that of the trivial solution (i.e., Minkowski metric with zero Maxwell and scalar fields) near each end at an appropriate inverse polynomial rate in rr (by definition, r→∞r\to\infty near an asymptotically flat end).

  • •

    It is in fact necessary for the initial hypersurface to have two asymptotically flat ends in order to support a non-vanishing charge (or equivalently, a nontrivial spherically symmetric Maxwell field).

  • •

    The future admissibility condition (see Definition 3.1.(5)), which was introduced in [15], is a natural generalization of the “no anti-trapped surfaces” condition of Christodoulou to the 2-ended case. See Steps 1 and 2(a) below for further discussion of its significance.

It turns out that the precise nature of the strong cosmic censorship that holds depends on the rates for which the scalar field decays near the asymptotically ends. In the introduction, in order to simplify the exposition, we will only consider1212 12 As we will see in Theorem 3.18, our methods also apply to the case 2<ω0<32<\omega_{0}<3, although the result will be qualitatively different. The significance of the number 33 is that it is the sharp Price’s law decay rate; assuming faster decay rates of the initial ϕ\phi and its derivatives does not improve the decay rate of the future development in general. the case where ϕ=O⁡(r−ω0)\phi=O(r^{-\omega_{0}}) near each asymptotically flat end, with ω0≥3\omega_{0}\geq 3.

On the space of admissible initial data sets, we define a scale of weighted-CkC^{k}-type distances (see Definition 3.5). The notion of genericity used in the precise version of Theorem 1.5 (see Theorem 3.14 and the ensuing statements) is defined (roughly) as being open relative to a weighted-C1C^{1}-type distance, and dense relative to a weighted-C∞C^{\infty}-type distance.

The proof of Theorem 1.5 can be roughly divided into the following five steps:

Step 1: An a priori boundary characterization [35] (Theorem 4.1). Thanks to the future admissibility and asymptotic flatness conditions, we may apply a result of [35] (or more precisely, by an adaptation of [35] to the 22-ended case in [15]) to show that the maximal globally hyperbolic future development (ℳ,g,ϕ,F)(\mathcal{M},g,\phi,F) of every admissible initial data set must have a black hole (interior) region ℬ=ℬi1+∪ℬi2+∪ℬn​o​n​p​e​r​t\mathscr{B}=\mathscr{B}_{i^{+}_{1}}\cup\mathscr{B}_{i^{+}_{2}}\cup\mathscr{B}_{nonpert}1313 13 For the definition of ℬi1+\mathscr{B}_{i^{+}_{1}}, ℬi2+\mathscr{B}_{i^{+}_{2}}, see Step 2(b). Then we define ℬn​o​n​p​e​r​t=ℬ∖(ℬi1+∪ℬi2+)\mathscr{B}_{nonpert}=\mathscr{B}\setminus(\mathscr{B}_{i^{+}_{1}}\cup\mathscr{B}_{i^{+}_{2}}). and an exterior region ℰ=ℰ1∪ℰ2\mathscr{E}=\mathscr{E}_{1}\cup\mathscr{E}_{2} with 22 connected components ℰ1\mathscr{E}_{1}, ℰ2\mathscr{E}_{2} corresponding to the 22 asymptotically flat ends of the initial hypersurface. Each connected component of the exterior region has a complete future null infinity (denoted by ℐ1+\mathcal{I}^{+}_{1} and ℐ2+\mathcal{I}^{+}_{2}, respectively) and approaches a connected component of the exterior region of a subextremal Reissner–Nordström spacetime. Moreover, the future boundary of the black hole region can be characterized. In fact, using also the results of [14] and the fact that the charge is non-vanishing, the quotient 𝒬=ℳ/S​O​(3)\mathcal{Q}=\mathcal{M}/SO(3) of the maximal globally hyperbolic future development must be given by one of the two Penrose diagrams in Figure 2, where we refer the reader to Theorem 4.1 for the notation.

Combining this theorem with results in [14, 18], it can be shown that the only way that the spacetime can be C2C^{2}-future-extendible is if there is an extension “through the Cauchy horizons 𝒞​ℋ1+∪𝒞​ℋ2+\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}\cup\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2}”. This is what we will have to rule out in the generic scenario.

Step 2: Convergence to Reissner–Nordström. In order for the linear analysis in [38] to be relevant to the nonlinear problem, it needs to be shown that the maximal globally hyperbolic development of every admissible initial data set in fact converges to Reissner--Nordström1414 14 Note that potentially, the solution approaches two different Reissner–Nordström solutions (i.e., with different parameters of the final masses) “towards two timelike infinities i1+i^{+}_{1}, i2+i^{+}_{2}.” with sufficiently strong estimates. This step is further divided into two substeps.

  • •

    Step 2(a): Price’s law decay in the exterior region [18] (Theorem 1.11, Theorem 4.4 or [36, Section 5]). In the exterior region ℰ1∪ℰ2\mathscr{E}_{1}\cup\mathscr{E}_{2}, since the event horizons are subextremal, the seminal work of Dafermos–Rodnianski shows that the spacetime approaches Reissner–Nordström and the scalar field (and its derivatives) decays with an inverse polynomial rate. In our setting, we will also need some refinements of the theorem of Dafermos–Rodnianski, for which we refer the reader to [36, Section 5].

  • •

    Step 2(b): C0C^{0}-stability in the interior region (Theorem 5.1). In view of the instability result we ultimately prove, in the interior we can only to hope1515 15 We will in fact show that the scalar field is not in Wl​o​c1,2W^{1,2}_{loc} in a C0C^{0} extension of the spacetime (cf. Theorem 5.4). In view of the result for the linear wave equation in [26], one expects in general that the scalar field is not even in Wl​o​c1,pW^{1,p}_{loc} for any p>1p>1. Here, the significance of the regularity C2C^{2} is that it allows us to pointwisely make sense of the curvature tensor (which is a geometric invariant), whose possible blow up is directly connected with that of the scalar field through the Einstein–Maxwell–(real)–scalar–field system (1.1).

More precisely, recall from Step 1 that the goal is to rule out any C2C^{2} future extensions through the Cauchy horizon. We refer the reader to Sections 3-7 for precise statements that are proven for each of these steps and how they fit together.

1.2. Previous works

In this subsection, we provide a brief survey of some previous works to place our main result (Theorem 1.5) and the ideas of its proof in context.

1.2.1. Linear wave equation on Reissner–Nordström spacetime

The simplest setting to study the stability and instability properties of the Cauchy horizon in the interior of Reissner–Nordström spacetime is to consider the linear scalar wave equation □gR​N​ϕ=0\Box_{g_{RN}}\phi=0 where the background Reissner–Nordström metric gR​Ng_{RN} is fixed. This problem has a long tradition in the physics literature and has attracted much renewed recent interest from the mathematical community. We refer the reader to [4, 21, 25, 26, 27, 29, 39, 40, 50, 48] for a sample of results and to the introduction of [38] for further discussions. In the interior of the black hole, solutions to the linear wave equation exhibit both stability and instabilty properties. While ϕ\phi itself is uniformly bounded and in fact decays along the Cauchy horizon [25, 29], the derivative of ϕ\phi in a direction transversal to the Cauchy horizon blows up. Indeed, we have the following instability result:

Theorem 1.7 (Linear instability on fixed Reissner–Nordström, Luk–Oh [38]).

Generic smooth and compactly supported initial data to the linear wave equation □gR​N​ϕ=0\Box_{g_{RN}}\phi=0 on a 22-ended asymptotically flat complete Cauchy hypersurface of a fixed subextremal Reissner–Nordström spacetime with nonvanishing charge give rise to solutions that are not in Wl​o​c1,2W^{1,2}_{loc} in a neighborhood of any point on the future Cauchy horizon 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}.

As we already discussed in Section 1.1, the methods introduced in [38] also play a crucial role in establishing instability for the nonlinear problem in spherical symmetry considered in this paper and [36]. Theorem 1.7 is proven via showing that the spherically symmetric part of a solution arising from generic smooth and compactly supported initial data is not in Wl​o​c1,2W^{1,2}_{loc} in a neighborhood of any point on the future Cauchy horizon. Its proof has the following three parts2222 22 These concern only one of the two asymptotically flat ends of Reissner–Nordström. An analogue of each part holds in the other end. In particular, the solution we construct in (3) can be made to vanish on the other component of the exterior region, and (by linearity) one can therefore easily add to it a solution that blows up on the “outgoing” part of the Cauchy horizon, constructed in essentially the same manner, so as to ensure that the solution blows up on the whole Cauchy horizon.:

  1. (1)

    It is shown that in the interior of the black hole region if an L2L^{2}-averaged polynomial lower bound holds for the spherically symmetric part of the solution on the event horizon, then the solution is not in Wl​o​c1,2W^{1,2}_{loc} in a neighborhood of any point on the future Cauchy horizon.

  2. (2)

    Moreover, a quantity2323 23 Notice that in the present paper, we introduce in addition the notation 𝔏(ω0)​∞\mathfrak{L}_{(\omega_{0})\infty}, which coincides with 𝔏\mathfrak{L} (in both this paper and [38]) for solutions arising from compactly supported initial data. 𝔏\mathfrak{L} at future null infinity associated to the spherically symmetric part of the solution is identified in [38]. The quantity 𝔏\mathfrak{L}, which is real-valued and depends linearly on ϕ\phi, moreover has the property that whenever 𝔏≠0\mathfrak{L}\neq 0, the L2L^{2}-averaged polynomial lower bound for the solution on the event horizon required in part (1) holds.

  3. (3)

    Finally, it is shown that 𝔏\mathfrak{L} is generically non-vanishing, by exhibiting a spherically symmetric solution to the linear wave equation with smooth compactly supported initial data on Σ0\Sigma_{0} for which 𝔏≠0\mathfrak{L}\neq 0.

In the language of Section 1.1, Steps 3(b), 3(a) and 4 can be viewed as analogues of (1), (2) and (3) above, respectively, but in a nonlinear setting.

1.2.2. Nonlinear stability and instability of the Cauchy horizon in spherical symmetry

Going beyond the linear wave equation, the next simplest problem is to consider a nonlinear model but restricted to spherical symmetry2424 24 Recall that Reissner–Nordström is spherically symmetric.. In part due to the fact that both stable and unstable features can be seen in the linear theory, the nature of the “singularity” that arises from perturbing Reissner–Nordström has been widely debated. In particular, it was speculated that nonlinear perturbations of Reissner–Nordström initial data may lead to a spacelike singularity. The study of the stability and instability of the Reissner–Nordström Cauchy horizon was initiated in the pioneering works of Hiscock [30], Poisson–Israel [45, 46] and Ori [42], who studied the Einstein equation coupled with null dusts in spherical symmetry. These works suggest that under nonlinear perturbations, the spacetime is regular up to the Cauchy horizon, which is in particular null, and the spacetime metric extends continuously to the Cauchy horizon. Nevertheless, generically, the metric “blows up” in the sense that the Hawking mass (described in Remark 1.10 below) is identically infinite on the Cauchy horizon.

The stability and instability of the Reissner--Nordström Cauchy horizon was finally settled mathematically in the seminal work2525 25 See also [11, 10, 34] for recent extensions of the results of Dafermos. of Dafermos [14] (see also [12]) in the context of the characteristic initial value problem for the Einstein–Maxwell–(real)–scalar field system posed in the black hole interior. He showed that for all initial data on the event horizon approaching Reissner–Nordström sufficiently fast, in a neighborhood of timelike infinity, the spacetime has a null boundary such that the metric remains continuous. In particular, when sufficiently close to timelike infinity, there are no “first singularities” arising before the null boundary. The instability of the smooth Cauchy horizon as suggested by the strong cosmic censorship conjecture only manifests itself in that for a “large subset” of admissible initial data, the null boundary is also a null singularity such that the metric cannot be extended beyond in C1C^{1} in spherical symmetry (see further discussions in [14]). We summarize the stability result in [14] as follows2626 26 In [14], the decay rate for ϕ\phi is not needed. Also, there is a version of the result requiring only s>12s>\frac{1}{2}. We state here only a version that is easy to compare with Theorem 5.1 in which we do not optimize the necessary decay rate on the event horizon. This is in particular because the results in [18] show that the bound holds for some s>1s>1 for solutions arising from asymptotically flat Cauchy data.:

Theorem 1.8 (Stability theorem, Dafermos [14]).

Fix MM, 𝐞{\bf e} and ss such that 0<|𝐞|<M0<|{\bf e}|<M and s>1s>1. Consider the characteristic initial value problem with smooth data given on C−∞C_{-\infty} and C¯1\underline{C}_{1} such that C−∞C_{-\infty} approaches the event horizon of Reissner–Nordström with 𝐞{\bf e} and MM and such that in an “Eddington–Finkelstein type” coordinate system, we have

(|ϕ|+|∂vϕ|)↾C−∞(v)≤Ev−s.(|\phi|+|\partial_{v}\phi|)\restriction_{C_{-\infty}}(v)\leq Ev^{-s}.

Then, by restricting to some nonempty, connected subset C¯1′⊂C¯1\underline{C}^{\prime}_{1}\subset\underline{C}_{1}, the globally hyperbolic future development of the data on C¯1′∪C−∞\underline{C}^{\prime}_{1}\cup C_{-\infty} has a Penrose diagram given by Figure 3. Moreover, the area-radius function rr and the scalar field ϕ\phi extend continuously to the Cauchy horizon 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}.

The stability theorem in [14] is complemented by the following conditional instability result:

Theorem 1.9 (Conditional instability theorem, Dafermos [14]).

If, in addition to the assumptions in Theorem 1.8, there exists ϵ>0\epsilon>0, c>0c>0 and v∗≥1v_{*}\geq 1 such that the following pointwise lower bound holds :

|∂vϕ|↾C−∞(v)≥cv−3​s+ϵ|\partial_{v}\phi|\restriction_{C_{-\infty}}(v)\geq cv^{-3s+\epsilon}

for all v≥v∗v\geq v_{*} (with ss as in Theorem 1.8), then the Hawking mass is identically infinite along the Cauchy horizon 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}.

Remark 1.10.

The Hawking mass described above is a geometric invariant for spherically symmetric spacetimes on every orbit of the S​O​(3)SO(3) action (see (2.6)). The infinitude of the Hawking mass is an obstruction to extending the spacetime in spherical symmetry with a C1C^{1} metric. Moreover, it can be shown [35] in this setting that the blow up of the Hawking mass implies the blow up of the Kretschmann scalar, which is an obstruction to extending the metric in C2C^{2} without assuming spherical symmetry for the extension. Note that in contrast to Theorem 1.9, our proof of Theorem 1.5 does not show the blow up of the Hawking mass, but instead requires a different geometric argument, cf. Step 5 in Section 1.1.

1.2.3. Nonlinear Price’s law and the disproof of the C0C^{0}-formulation of strong cosmic censorship in spherical symmetry

The preceding two results of Dafermos in the black hole interior assume inverse polynomial decay rates of the scalar field along the event horizon as upper and lower bounds (in Theorems 1.8 and 1.9, respectively). These assumptions are consistent with a well-established heuristics called Price’s law, which predicts that any asymptotically flat perturbation of Reissner–Nordström leads to a scalar field with a specific inverse-polynomial upper bound on the event horizon (namely, |ϕ|≤v−3|\phi|\leq v^{-3} and |∂vϕ|≤v−4|\partial_{v}\phi|\leq v^{-4} for an “Eddington–Finkelstein type” coordinate vv), and that the same inverse-polynomial lower bound holds in the “generic” case.

Price’s law was derived via a heuristic linear analysis, and recently there have been numerous works on its rigorous proof in the context of the linear wave equation on the exterior of a black hole spacetime. We refer the reader to [22, 23, 24, 1, 2, 51, 41] for a sample of such results. Remarkably, in the nonlinear context of the Einstein–Maxwell–(real)–scalar–field system in spherical symmetry, Dafermos–Rodnianski [18] were able to establish the upper bound assertion of Price’s law for the maximal development of any admissible initial data, which may in principle be very far from a small perturbation of Reissner–Nordström. We summarize a part of their theorem which is relevant for the current discussion as follows:

Theorem 1.11 (Price’s law, Dafermos–Rodnianski [18]).

Consider smooth spherically symmetric 2-ended Cauchy initial data for (1.1), which are future-admissible and asymptotically flat (cf. Definition 3.1). Then the maximal globally hyperbolic future development obeys

|ϕ|+|∂vϕ|↾ℋ1+(v)≤Esv−s,|\phi|+|\partial_{v}\phi|\restriction_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}(v)\leq E_{s}v^{-s},

for any s<3s<3 and for some Es>0E_{s}>0, where vv is an “Eddington–Finkelstein type” advanced null coordinate on the event horizon ℋ1+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1} (cf. Definition 4.2). An analogous statement holds on the event horizon ℋ2+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2} corresponding to the other asymptotically flat end.

For more a precise statement and further discussions, see Step 2(a) in Section 1.1, Theorem 4.4 and [36, Section 5].

Combining Theorem 1.11 with the interior stability result (Theorem 1.8), one reaches the striking conclusion that the C0C^{0}-formulation of the strong cosmic censorship conjecture for the Einstein–Maxwell–(real)–scalar–field system in spherical symmetry is false (Theorem 1.4).

1.2.4. Comparisons with an approach based on Theorem 1.9 in [14]

Given the interior instability result (Theorem 1.9) and Price’s law, one obvious path to proving the C2C^{2}-formulation of the strong cosmic censorship conjecture (Theorem 1.5) would be to establish the assumed pointwise lower bound in Theorem 1.9 for maximal globally hyperbolic future developments of generic data. In a recent work of Angelopoulos–Aretakis–Gajic [1], the authors proved an analogous lower bound2727 27 In fact, they obtained a much stronger result giving the precise asymptotics of the solution. In particular, they proved upper and lower bounds for ∂vϕ\partial_{v}\phi along the event horizon with the same rate predicted by Price’s law. for generic solutions to the linear wave equation on a fixed subextremal Reissner–Nordström spacetime with non-vanishing charge. In view of this, one may conjecture that the same lower bound holds for generic data in our nonlinear setting in spherical symmetry:

Conjecture 1.12.

There exists a generic set of spherically symmetric admissible Cauchy initial data with non-vanishing charge (cf. Definition 3.1) and compactly supported initial scalar field such that the lower bound in Theorem 1.9 holds with s=3s=3 on each of the event horizons in the maximal globally hyperbolic future developments.

As discussed in Section 1.1, however, we take a different route and instead prove a stronger conditional instability result which requires an L2L^{2}-averaged, instead of a pointwise, lower bound. The upshot is that such an L2L^{2}-averaged lower bound is considerably easier (even though it is still highly technical) to prove. In particular, even to prove the lower bound in the linear setting in [1], it first requires sharp upper bound estimates. Such estimates would be even harder to obtain in the nonlinear setting in view of the fact that we are considering large data solutions. In contrast, with our approach, in terms of the decay rates of a fixed solution, it suffices to use the Dafermos–Rodnianski decay theorem in [18], in which the decay rates are conjecturally2828 28 At the very least, it is known by [1] that the upper bounds in [18] are not sharp for solutions to the linear wave equation. not sharp.

While the main motivation for our improved conditional instability theorem is that it is easier to verify than the condition in [14], it should be noted that our approach based on the new conditional instability theorem also provides a road map for proving instability for other matter models and for the vacuum equations without symmetry. This is because in the problem of, say, the instability of the Reissner–Nordström Cauchy horizon in spherical symmetry for the Einstein–Maxwell–charged–(complex)–scalar field model, or in the problem of the instability of the Kerr Cauchy horizon without symmetry condition for the Einstein vacuum equations, the generic solutions along the event horizon are expected to be oscillatory [31, 32, 33, 3, 43]. This is in contrast to the type of behavior that is required by [14], but on the other hand is consistent with the condition that we require in our approach.

1.3. Outline of the paper

We end the introduction with an outline of the remainder of the paper.

  • •

    In Section 2, we introduce the setup for the Einstein–Maxwell–(real)–scalar–field system in spherical symmetry.

  • •

    In Section 3, we give the precise formulation of strong cosmic censorship (Theorem 1.5, cf. Theorems 3.14, 3.18 and Corollary 3.21).

The next few sections are dedicated to the main steps of the proof of Theorem 1.5:

  • •

    In Section 4, we discuss previous results of Kommemi [35] and Dafermos–Rodnianski [18] regarding the maximal globally hyperbolic development.

  • •

    In Section 5, we give the precise statements of the main theorems (Theorems 5.1, 5.4, 5.5 and 5.7) proved in this paper regarding the interior region.

  • •

    In Section 6, we discuss the results in [36] regarding the exterior region.

  • •

    In Section 7, combining the results of Sections 5 and 6, we obtain a proof of Theorems 3.14, 3.18 and Corollary 3.21.

The remaining sections contain the proofs of the theorems:

  • •

    In Section 8, we prove the stability theorem (Theorem 5.1).

  • •

    In Section 9, we prove the instability theorem (Theorem 5.4).

  • •

    In Section 10, the stability and instability theorems are then “globalized” (Theorem 5.5).

  • •

    In Section 11, we prove the theorem on C2C^{2} future-inextendibility (Theorem 5.7).

Finally, we have an appendix with three sections.

  • •

    In Appendix A, we give a proof of Kommemi’s theorem that the limits along the event horizons are always subextremal in the model under consideration. In Appendix B, we give a discussion regarding the gauge condition that we impose on the event horizon. In Appendix C, we study in more detail the blow-up behavior of the solution in the C0C^{0} extension constructed in Theorems 5.1 and 5.5, and show that the Christoffel symbols fail to be locally LpL^{p}-integrable for every p>1p>1.

2. Einstein–Maxwell–(real)–scalar–field system in spherical symmetry

The purpose of this preliminary section is to provide the precise setup for the model at hand, namely the Einstein–Maxwell–(real)–scalar–field system in spherical symmetry. We begin with the definition of spherical symmetry in our context.

Definition 2.1 (Spherically symmetric solutions).

Let (ℳ,g,ϕ,F)(\mathcal{M},g,\phi,F) be a suitably regular2929 29 The precise regularity is irrelevant here, since the notion of solutions we work with will be defined later with respect to the reduced system in spherical symmetry. See the well-posedness statements in Propositions 2.4 and 2.5. solution to the Einstein–Maxwell–(real)–scalar–field system (1.1). We say that (ℳ,g,ϕ,F)(\mathcal{M},g,\phi,F) is spherically symmetric if the following properties hold:

    r=Area​(𝝅−1​(p))4​π,r=\sqrt{\frac{\mbox{Area}({\boldsymbol{\pi}}^{-1}(p))}{4\pi}},

    for every p∈𝒬p\in\mathcal{Q}, where 𝝅{\boldsymbol{\pi}} is natural projection 𝝅:ℳ→𝒬{\boldsymbol{\pi}}:\mathcal{M}\to\mathcal{Q} taking a point to the group orbit it belongs to. Here, as in the introduction, d​σ𝕊2d\sigma_{\mathbb{S}^{2}} denotes the standard round metric on 𝕊2\mathbb{S}^{2} with radius 11.

  3. (3)

    The function ϕ\phi at a point xx depends only on 𝝅⁡(x){\boldsymbol{\pi}}(x), i.e., for p∈𝒬p\in\mathcal{Q} and x,y∈𝝅−1​(p)x,y\in{\boldsymbol{\pi}}^{-1}(p), it holds that ϕ⁡(x)=ϕ⁡(y)\phi(x)=\phi(y).

    The Maxwell field FF is invariant under pullback by the action (by isometry) of S​O​(3)SO(3) on ℳ\mathcal{M}. Moreover, there exists 𝐞:𝒬→ℝ{\bf e}:\mathcal{Q}\to\mathbb{R} such that

In spherical symmetry, the Einstein-Maxwell-(real)-scalar-field system thus reduces to the following system of coupled wave equations for (r,ϕ,Ω)(r,\phi,\Omega)

{∂u∂vr=−Ω24​r−∂ur​∂vrr+Ω2​𝐞24​r3,∂u∂vϕ=−∂vr​∂uϕr−∂ur​∂vϕr,∂u∂vlog⁡Ω=−∂uϕ∂vϕ−Ω2​𝐞22​r4+Ω24​r2+∂ur​∂vrr2.\left\{\begin{aligned} \partial_{u}\partial_{v}r=&-\frac{\Omega^{2}}{4r}-\frac{\partial_{u}r\partial_{v}r}{r}+\frac{\Omega^{2}{\bf e}^{2}}{4r^{3}},\\ \partial_{u}\partial_{v}\phi=&-\frac{\partial_{v}r\partial_{u}\phi}{r}-\frac{\partial_{u}r\partial_{v}\phi}{r},\\ \partial_{u}\partial_{v}\log\Omega=&-\partial_{u}\phi\partial_{v}\phi-\frac{\Omega^{2}{\bf e}^{2}}{2r^{4}}+\frac{\Omega^{2}}{4r^{2}}+\frac{\partial_{u}r\partial_{v}r}{r^{2}}.\end{aligned}\right. 3. Formulation of strong cosmic censorship

In this section we give a precise formulation of strong cosmic censorship for maximal globally hyperbolic future development of admissible initial data (Theorem 3.14, see also Theorem 3.18). Before that, we need to introduce three important notions:

  • •

    A class of admissible Cauchy data: This includes the assumptions of the regularity and asymptotic flatness of the initial data. We will impose an additional future admissibility condition, see the last point in Definition 3.1, which can be thought of as an analogue of Christodoulou’s “no anti-trapped surface” condition suitably adapted to the case of 22-ended asymptotically flat data, see [15]. This will be introduced in Section 3.1.

  • •

    Topologies on the set of admissible Cauchy data: The various topologies will allow us to make precise the genericity condition, which can be understood as openness and density statements in appropriate topologies. This will be introduced in Section 3.2.

  • •

    The constants 𝔏(ω)​∞\mathfrak{L}_{(\omega)\infty} and 𝔏(ω)​∞′\mathfrak{L}^{\prime}_{(\omega)\infty}: For every admissible Cauchy data set, the constants 𝔏(ω)​∞\mathfrak{L}_{(\omega)\infty} and 𝔏(ω)​∞′\mathfrak{L}_{(\omega)\infty}^{\prime} are introduced to give an easy-to-check criterion which, when verified, would guarantee that the maximal globally hyperbolic future development is C2C^{2}-future-inextendible. These constants will be featured in the statement of strong cosmic censorship and will be introduced in Section 3.3.

We will then give the main statement of strong cosmic censorship in Section 3.4. This is followed in Section 3.5 by a (much) simpler statement if a sufficiently slowly decaying inverse polynomial tail is allowed in the initial data. We will end the section with a discussion on the global stability and instability of the Reissner–Nordström Cauchy horizon in Section 3.6. All of the results stated in this section will be proven in Section 7.

3.1. Admissible Cauchy data

We now define the class of Cauchy initial data for which we will establish strong cosmic censorship.

Definition 3.1 (Admissible Cauchy initial data).

Let ω0>2\omega_{0}>2. An ω0\omega_{0}-future-admissible spherically symmetric 22-ended asymptotically flat Cauchy initial data set with non-vanishing charge (in short, an ω0\omega_{0}-admissible initial data set) is a Cauchy initial data set Θ=(r,f,h,ℓ,ϕ,ϕ˙,𝐞)\Theta=(r,f,h,\ell,\phi,\dot{\phi},{\bf e}) on Σ0=ℝ\Sigma_{0}=\mathbb{R} satisfying the following properties:

  1. (1)

    ϕ,f∈C2​(Σ0,ℝ)\phi,\,f\in C^{2}(\Sigma_{0};\mathbb{R}), ϕ˙,h∈C1​(Σ0,ℝ)\dot{\phi},\,h\in C^{1}(\Sigma_{0};\mathbb{R}) (i.e., are more regular3333 33 Note that while the regularity assumptions in Definition 2.2 are sufficient for the local existence and uniqueness result in Proposition 2.4 (and it fact also for global decay result, see [18]), we need additional regularity in order to control the difference of the gauges in two different solutions in [36]. This is of course unsurprising in view of the quasilinear nature of the problem. than required in Definition 2.2).

    Here the notation Oi​(|ρ|−n)O_{i}(|\rho|^{-n}) denotes that the function on the LHS is O⁡(|ρ|−n)O(|\rho|^{-n}) and the jj-th derivative is O⁡(|ρ|−n−j)O(|\rho|^{-n-j}) for all j≤ij\leq i. In the case n=0n=0, we simply write Oi​(1)=Oi​(|ρ|0)O_{i}(1)=O_{i}(|\rho|^{0}). The notation Oi​(log⁡|ρ|)O_{i}(\log|\rho|) is defined similarly.

    ϕ⁡(ρ)=O2​(|ρ|−ω0),ϕ˙​(ρ)=O1​(|ρ|−ω0−1).\phi(\rho)=O_{2}(|\rho|^{-\omega_{0}}),\quad\dot{\phi}(\rho)=O_{1}(|\rho|^{-\omega_{0}-1}). (3.2)

Remark 3.2 (Future admissibility condition in double null coordinates).

By Lemma 2.3, the future admissibility condition can be understood as requiring that (∂ur)↾Σ0(ρ)<0(\partial_{u}r)\restriction_{\Sigma_{0}}(\rho)<0 for ρ≥ρ1\rho\geq\rho_{1} and (∂vr)↾Σ0(ρ)<0(\partial_{v}r)\restriction_{\Sigma_{0}}(\rho)<0 for ρ≤ρ2\rho\leq\rho_{2}. Remark 3.3 (Stability of future admissibility condition).

The future admissibility condition is manifestly stable against small perturbations (say, with respect to the distances defined in Section 3.2).

Example 3.4 (Reissner–Nordström initial data).

An example of an ω0\omega_{0}-future-admissible Cauchy initial data in the sense of Definition 3.1 (for any ω0>2\omega_{0}>2) is the Cauchy initial data set of a subextremal Reissner–Nordström solution with 𝐞≠0{\bf e}\neq 0 on a suitable initial hypersurface Σ0¯\underline{\Sigma_{0}}. More precisely, we take Σ0¯\underline{\Sigma_{0}} to be a (sufficiently smooth) spherically symmetric Cauchy hypersurface that intersects the black hole region (shaded region in Figure 4). Note that ϕ=ϕ˙=0\phi=\dot{\phi}=0 in this case. We also note that, by (an extension of) Birkhoff’s theorem for the Einstein–Maxwell system, any admissible initial data set satisfying Definition 3.1 with ϕ=ϕ˙=0\phi=\dot{\phi}=0 is necessarily an embedded Cauchy hypersurface in some subextremal Reissner–Nordström solution.

3.4. Statement of the strong cosmic censorship theorem in spherical symmetry

Before we give the statement of strong cosmic censorship, we need to make precise the notion of C2C^{2}-future-inextendibility:

Definition 3.12 (C2C^{2}-future-inextendibility).

A C2C^{2} Lorentzian 44-manifold (ℳ,g)(\mathcal{M},g) is said to be future-extendible with a C2C^{2} Lorentzian metric if there exists a time-oriented, connected C2C^{2} Lorentzian 44-manifold (ℳ~,g~)(\widetilde{\mathcal{M}},\tilde{g}) and an isometric embedding ι:ℳ→ℳ~\iota:\mathcal{M}\to\widetilde{\mathcal{M}} such that ι⁡(ℳ)\iota(\mathcal{M}) is a proper subset of ℳ~\widetilde{\mathcal{M}} and moreover for every p∈ℳ~∖ℳp\in\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}\setminus\mathcal{M}, I+​(p)∩ℳ=∅I^{+}(p)\cap\mathcal{M}=\emptyset. (ℳ,g)(\mathcal{M},g) is said to be future-inextendible with a C2C^{2} Lorentzian metric (in short, C2C^{2}-future-inextendible) otherwise.

Definition 3.13 (C2C^{2}-future-inextendibility of solutions to (1.1)).

We say that a solution (ℳ,g,ϕ,F)(\mathcal{M},g,\phi,F) to (1.1) is C2C^{2}-future-inextendible if the underlying Lorentzian manifold (ℳ,g)(\mathcal{M},g) is C2C^{2}-future-inextendible (as in Definition 3.12).

The following is the strong cosmic censorship theorem for ω0\omega_{0}-admissible initial data, with ω0≥3\omega_{0}\geq 3.

3.5. Strong cosmic censorship in the case 2<ω0<32<\omega_{0}<3

Our strategy also gives a strong cosmic censorship theorem for ω0\omega_{0}-admissible initial data with 2<ω0<32<\omega_{0}<3. In this case, however, the nature of the density statement is qualitatively different, since the backscattering effect (captured by 𝔏\mathfrak{L}) is too weak to modify the leading order tail of ∂v(r​ϕ)\partial_{v}(r\phi) near the future endpoint of ℐ+\mathcal{I}^{+} (captured by 𝔏(ω0)​∞\mathfrak{L}_{(\omega_{0})\infty}).

      if Θ¯∈Cω0k\overline{\Theta}\in C^{k}_{\omega_{0}} for k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, k≥2k\geq 2, ϵ↦Θϵ\epsilon\mapsto\Theta_{\epsilon} is continuous with respect to dk,ω0d_{k,\omega_{0}}.

Remark 3.19 (𝔏(ω0)​∞\mathfrak{L}_{(\omega_{0})\infty} depends only on the initial data for ω0∈(2,3)\omega_{0}\in(2,3)).

The proof of Theorem 3.18 is much simpler than its counterpart (Theorem 3.14) when ω0≥3\omega_{0}\geq 3. In fact, the philosophies of the proofs for Theorem 3.18 and Theorem 3.14 are rather different. For Theorem 3.18, since when ω0∈(2,3)\omega_{0}\in(2,3), 𝔏(ω0)​∞=𝔏(ω0)​0\mathfrak{L}_{(\omega_{0})\infty}=\mathfrak{L}_{(\omega_{0})0} and 𝔏(ω0)​∞′=𝔏(ω0)​0′\mathfrak{L}_{(\omega_{0})\infty}^{\prime}=\mathfrak{L}_{(\omega_{0})0}^{\prime} depend only on the initial data, it suffices to perturb the incoming part of the data with a (precise) polynomial tail to modify 𝔏(ω0)​0\mathfrak{L}_{(\omega_{0})0} and 𝔏(ω0)​0′\mathfrak{L}_{(\omega_{0})0}^{\prime}. In contrast, in the proof of Theorem 6.3 in [36], we add a (smooth) compactly supported perturbation to the outgoing part of the data to perturb the dynamically defined quantity 𝔏\mathfrak{L}, rather than 𝔏(ω0)​0\mathfrak{L}_{(\omega_{0})0} on Σ0\Sigma_{0}. On a technical level, in the case ω0∈(2,3)\omega_{0}\in(2,3), we can completely bypass Theorem 6.2, which is in some sense the most technically involved step of the proof.

Remark 3.20 (Topology of the initial data).

We note explicitly that the difference between the statements (3) in Theorem 3.14 and (3’) in Theorem 3.18 is that in (3’), the perturbations are only close to Θ¯\overline{\Theta} with respect to dk,ω0d_{k,\omega_{0}}, instead of with respect to dk,ωd_{k,\omega} for arbitrary ω>0\omega>0. This is because in the case ω0∈(2,3)\omega_{0}\in(2,3), we are forced to add in a polynomial tail to make 𝔏(ω0)​0\mathfrak{L}_{(\omega_{0})0} and 𝔏(ω0)​0′\mathfrak{L}^{\prime}_{(\omega_{0})0} non-zero. Any perturbation with a faster decay rate as r→∞r\to\infty cannot alter 𝔏(ω0)​∞\mathfrak{L}_{(\omega_{0})\infty} and 𝔏(ω0)​0′\mathfrak{L}^{\prime}_{(\omega_{0})0}, which restricts the topology in (3’) to dk,ω0d_{k,\omega_{0}}.

3.6. Specializing to a (small) neighborhood of Reissner–Nordström

Since there exist Cauchy hypersurfaces in subextremal Reissner–Nordström spacetimes with non-vanishing charge for which the induced data are future-admissible (cf. Example 3.4) and the admissibility condition is a stable property (cf. Remark 3.3), it follows a fortiori from Theorem 3.14 that there exist arbitrarily small perturbations of Reissner–Nordström data such that the maximal globally hyperbolic future developments are C2C^{2}-future-inextendible.

In fact, more can be said in the case of solutions arising from small perturbations of Reissner–Nordström data. First, a result of Dafermos [15] shows that the interior of the black hole (and similarly the white hole) has a global bifurcate Cauchy horizon and the boundary does not contain any spacelike portion. (In the language of Theorem 4.1 in Section 4 below, this means that 𝒮=∅\mathcal{S}=\emptyset.) Second, though perhaps not so physically relevant, one can use the main theorem together with Cauchy stability to obtain the following result on the instability of Reissner–Nordström, which is global to the future and to the past:

Corollary 3.21 (Instability of Reissner–Nordström).

Given (M,𝐞)(M,{\bf e}) with 0<|𝐞|<M0<|{\bf e}|<M, there exists a sequence (Θi)i∈ℕ(\Theta_{i})_{i\in\mathbb{N}} of smooth perturbations of Reissner–Nordström data with parameters MM and 𝐞{\bf e} such that

  • •

    Θi∈𝒜​ℐ​𝒟​(ω)∩Cω∞\Theta_{i}\in\mathcal{A}\mathcal{I}\mathcal{D}(\omega)\cap C^{\infty}_{\omega} for all ω>2\omega>2, for all i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N} (cf. Definition 3.1 and Remark 3.17).

  • •

    The initial data for ϕ\phi and ϕ˙\dot{\phi} for Θi\Theta_{i} are compactly supported for all i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N}. Moreover, “the support is uniformly bounded for all ii” in the sense that supi∈ℕsups​u​p​p​(ϕ)∪s​u​p​p​(ϕ˙)r<∞\displaystyle\sup_{i\in\mathbb{N}}\sup_{supp(\phi)\cup supp(\dot{\phi})}r<\infty.

  • •

    As i→∞i\to\infty, Θi→ΘR​N,M,𝐞\Theta_{i}\to\Theta_{RN,M,{\bf e}} with respect to the distance dωd_{\omega} for any ω>2\omega>2 (cf. Definition 3.7 and (3.8)).

  • •

    (Dafermos [15]) For each i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N}, the maximal globally hyperbolic future-and-past development arising from Θi\Theta_{i} has the identical Penrose diagram as a subextremal Reissner–Nordström spacetime, as depicted in Figure 4. In particular, it has global bifurcate Cauchy horizons both to the future and to the past.

  • •

    For every i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N}, the maximal globally hyperbolic future-and-past development are C2C^{2}-future-and-past-inextendible.

4. Maximal globally hyperbolic future development of admissible Cauchy data

We now begin discussing the ingredients of the proof of Theorem 3.14 (and Theorem 3.18 and Corollary 3.21). In the next few sections, we will build up to the proof in Section 7. In this section, we collect some known results regarding the maximal globally hyperbolic future development of admissible Cauchy data. This corresponds to Steps 1 and 2(a) in the discussion in Section 1.1 in the introduction.

We begin with a preliminary characterization of the future boundary of the maximal globally hyperbolic future development of an admissible data set can be obtained3737 37 The original theorem of Kommemi applies in the case with one asymptotically flat end. The ideas, however, can be applied in our setting, see discussions in [15]. from the work of Kommemi [35].

Let (ℳ,g,ϕ,F)(\mathcal{M},g,\phi,F) be the maximal globally hyperbolic future development of an admissible Cauchy initial data set (with arbitrary ω0>2\omega_{0}>2, cf.       Two connected components of null infinity, denoted by ℐ1+\mathcal{I}^{+}_{1} and ℐ2+\mathcal{I}^{+}_{2} respectively, each of which is an open null segment4040 40 The fact that it is open and that rr does not diverge to ∞\infty along ℋ1+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1} and ℋ2+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2} (see Definition 4.2 below), follows from [13]., defined as the part of the boundary such that the rr diverges to ∞\infty along a transversal null curve towards ℐ1+\mathcal{I}^{+}_{1} and ℐ2+\mathcal{I}^{+}_{2}.

4.1. Subextremality of the event horizons

Given the boundary characterization, one can define the event horizons, see Definition 4.2. We will recall a result of Kommemi that under the admissibility condition, the event horizons are subextremal, see Proposition 4.3. The most important consequence of the subextremality statement is that the Price’s law decay of Dafermos–Rodnianski applies. We will discuss this in the next subsection.

We now begin with the definition of the event horizons. For this, introduce the notation u¯​(v)\underline{u}(v) and v¯​(u)\underline{v}(u) so that (u,v¯​(u)),(u¯​(v),v)∈Σ0(u,\underline{v}(u)),(\underline{u}(v),v)\in\Sigma_{0}.

Definition 4.2 (Event horizons).

Given the maximal globally hyperbolic future development of an admissible Cauchy initial data set (with arbitrary ω>2\omega>2, cf. Definition 3.1), define the event horizon ℋ1+:={(u,v):u=uℋ1+,v≥v¯(uℋ+)}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}:=\{(u,v):u=u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}},\,v\geq\underline{v}(u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}})\}, where uℋ1+:=sup{u:supr⁡(u′,⋅)=∞​ for all ​u′<u}u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}:=\sup\{u:\sup r(u^{\prime},\cdot)=\infty\mbox{ for all }u^{\prime}<u\} and v¯​(uℋ+)\underline{v}(u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}}) is such that (uℋ+,v¯​(uℋ+))∈Σ0(u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}},\underline{v}(u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}}))\in\Sigma_{0}. Abusing notation, we will also refer to the set ℋ1+×𝕊2⊂ℳ\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}\times\mathbb{S}^{2}\subset\mathcal{M} as the event horizon. Notice that this is well-defined by Theorem 4.1 and can be viewed as the past-directed null curve emanating from i1+i^{+}_{1}.

We also define the event horizon ℋ2+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2} emanating from i2+i^{+}_{2} in a completely analogous manner, namely, ℋ2+:={(u,v):v=vℋ2+,u≥u¯(vℋ2+)}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2}:=\{(u,v):v=v_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2}},\,u\geq\underline{u}(v_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2}})\}, where vℋ2+:=sup{v:supr⁡(⋅,v′)=∞​ for all ​v′<v}v_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2}}:=\sup\{v:\sup r(\cdot,v^{\prime})=\infty\mbox{ for all }v^{\prime}<v\} and u¯​(vℋ2+)\underline{u}(v_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2}}) is such that (u¯​(vℋ2+),vℋ2+)∈Σ0(\underline{u}(v_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2}}),v_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2}})\in\Sigma_{0}.

Importantly, the event horizons ℋ1+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1} and ℋ2+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2} are subextremal, in the sense that supϖ⁡(uℋ1+,⋅)>|𝐞|\sup\varpi(u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}},\cdot)>|{\bf e}| and supϖ⁡(⋅,vℋ2+)>|𝐞|\sup{\varpi(\cdot,v_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2}})}>|{\bf e|}. This is a result in the PhD thesis of Kommemi [34]. We include a proof in Appendix A for the convenience of the reader.

Proposition 4.3 (Subextremality of the event horizons, Kommemi [34]).

The following strict inequalities hold:

supϖ⁡(uℋ1+,⋅)>|𝐞|,supϖ⁡(⋅,vℋ2+)>|𝐞|.\sup\varpi(u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}},\cdot)>|{\bf e}|,\quad\sup\varpi(\cdot,v_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2}})>|{\bf e}|.

4.2. Price’s law decay theorem of Dafermos–Rodnianski

By the subextremality assertion (Proposition 4.3), the Price’s law decay theorem due to Dafermos–Rodnianski is applicable. For our purposes in this paper, it suffices to only state a subset of the estimates that are proven in [18].

Theorem 4.4 (Price’s law decay, Dafermos–Rodnianski [18]).

Let (ℳ,g,ϕ,F)(\mathcal{M},g,\phi,F) be the maximal globally hyperbolic future development of an admissible Cauchy initial data set with some ω0>2\omega_{0}>2 (cf. Definition 3.1). Let (u,v)(u,v) be a coordinate system defined in connected component of the exterior region bounded in the future by ℋ1+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1} and ℐ1+\mathcal{I}^{+}_{1} such that v=∞v=\infty at4444 44 This statement, and the statement ℋ1+={(u,v):u=∞}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}=\{(u,v):u=\infty\} is to be understood in terms of the conformal embedding of 𝒬\mathcal{Q} given in Theorem 4.1, i.e., for every fixed uu and a sequence vi→∞v_{i}\to\infty, (u,vi)(u,v_{i}) corresponds to a sequence of points converging to ℐ1+\mathcal{I}^{+}_{1} with respect to the topology induced by the conformal embedding. ℐ1+\mathcal{I}^{+}_{1} and u=∞u=\infty at ℋ1+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1} with the normalizations

limv→∞(−∂ur)1−μ​(u,v)=1,C0−1≤limu→∞∂vr1−μ​(u,v)≤C0,\lim_{v\to\infty}\frac{(-\partial_{u}r)}{1-\mu}(u,v)=1,\quad C_{0}^{-1}\leq\lim_{u\to\infty}\frac{\partial_{v}r}{1-\mu}(u,v)\leq C_{0}, (4.1)

for some constants C0C_{0}. Then, for every η>0\eta>0, there exists some B>0B>0 depending on C0C_{0}, η\eta, as well as the solution, such that the following (future) decay estimates hold along the event horizon ℋ1+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}:

|ϕ|​(∞,v)+|∂vϕ|​(∞,v)≤B​v−min⁡{ω,3}+ηfor ​v≥1|\phi|(\infty,v)+|\partial_{v}\phi|(\infty,v)\leq Bv^{-\min\{\omega,3\}+\eta}\quad\mbox{for }v\geq 1

and the following (future) decay estimates hold along future null infinity ℐ1+\mathcal{I}^{+}_{1}:

r​|ϕ|​(u,∞)≤B​u−min⁡{ω,3}+1for ​u≥1.r|\phi|(u,\infty)\leq Bu^{-\min\{\omega,3\}+1}\quad\mbox{for }u\geq 1.

An analogous statement obviously holds in the exterior region bounded in the future by ℋ2+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2} and ℐ2+\mathcal{I}^{+}_{2} with obvious modifications.

Remark 4.5 (Completeness of null infinity and event horizon).

It is implicit in Theorem 4.4 that both ℐ1+\mathcal{I}^{+}_{1} and ℋ1+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1} are complete4545 45 See [13] for a definition of the completeness of null infinity. This follows from the existence of double null coordinates u,vu,v which satisfy the normalization (4.1) and have infinite range, as required by Theorem 4.4.

Remark 4.6 (Applicability of Theorem 4.4 in our setting).

At this point, it may not be entirely obvious that the results in [18], which are originally stated for a characteristic initial value problem, are applicable in our setting where we start with a Cauchy initial data set. However, using asymptotic flatness, one can indeed reduce the problem to the characteristic initial value problem considered in [18]. Moreover, the existence of a double null coordinate system (u,v)(u,v) satisfying the conditions of Theorem 4.4 (and hence completeness of ℐ1+\mathcal{I}^{+}_{1} and ℋ1+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1} by Remark 4.5) can be proven. Detailed proofs of these statements can be found in [36, Section 5].

5. Main theorems for the interior region proven in this paper

In this section, we state the main theorems for the interior region. These are the precise versions of the results corresponding to Steps 2(b), 3(b), 3(c) and 5 in Section 1.1. These results will be proven in Section 8, 9, 10 and 11 respectively. We also refer the reader to the beginning of each of those sections for brief discussions of the ideas of the proofs.

5.1. Geometry of Reissner–Nordström interior

In this subsection, we briefly digress to discuss the geometry of the interior of Reissner–Nordström. This will provide the language and notations for some of the statements in the remainder of the paper.

Let 𝐞{\bf e} and MM be real numbers such that 0<|𝐞|<M0<|{\bf e}|<M. The interior of the Reissner–Nordström black hole is the manifold ℝ2×𝕊2\mathbb{R}^{2}\times\mathbb{S}^{2} together with the metric (1.2):

g=−(1−2​Mr+𝐞2r2)​d​t2+(1−2​Mr+𝐞2r2)−1​d​r2+r2​d​σ𝕊2,g=-\left(1-\frac{2M}{r}+\frac{{\bf e}^{2}}{r^{2}}\right)\,dt^{2}+\left(1-\frac{2M}{r}+\frac{{\bf e}^{2}}{r^{2}}\right)^{-1}\,dr^{2}+r^{2}d\sigma_{\mathbb{S}^{2}},

where rr ranges over (r−,r+)(r_{-},r_{+}) with r±:=M±M2−𝐞2r_{\pm}:=M\pm\sqrt{M^{2}-{\bf e}^{2}} and tt ranges over (−∞,∞)(-\infty,\infty). In Section 5.1.1, we will introduce a set of null coordinates (u,v)(u,v) and put the metric in the form (2.1), (2.2) as discussed in Section 2. We then introduce the notions of the event horizon and the Cauchy horizon in Section 5.1.2. In Sections 5.1.3 and 5.1.4, we will introduce two more systems of null coordinates, namely, the (U,v)(U,v) and (u,V)(u,V) coordinate system, which are regular at the event horizon and Cauchy horizon respectively. In the paper (especially in the proof of Theorem 5.1), we will use all of these coordinate systems to compare the metric of the spacetime solution in question with that of the Reissner–Nordström spacetime.

5.1.2. The event horizon and the Cauchy horizon

In this subsection, we introduce the event horizon and the Cauchy horizon. For this purpose, we will need to introduce a few additional sets of null coordinates. Define the functions Uℋ+​(u)U_{\mathcal{H}^{+}}(u), U𝒞​ℋ+​(u)U_{\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}}(u), Vℋ+​(v)V_{\mathcal{H}^{+}}(v) and V𝒞​ℋ+​(v)V_{\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}}(v) which are smooth and strictly increasing functions of their arguments and satisfy the following ODEs:

d​Uℋ+d​u=e2​κ+​u​ and ​Uℋ+​(u)→0​ as ​u→−∞;\frac{dU_{\mathcal{H}^{+}}}{du}=e^{2\kappa_{+}u}\mbox{ and }\,U_{\mathcal{H}^{+}}(u)\to 0\mbox{ as }u\to-\infty; (5.4)
d​U𝒞​ℋ+d​u=e−2​κ−​u​ and ​U𝒞​ℋ+​(u)→1​ as ​u→+∞;\frac{dU_{\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}}}{du}=e^{-2\kappa_{-}u}\mbox{ and }\,U_{\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}}(u)\to 1\mbox{ as }u\to+\infty; (5.5)
d​Vℋ+d​v=e2​κ+​v​ and ​Vℋ+​(v)→0​ as ​v→−∞;\frac{dV_{\mathcal{H}^{+}}}{dv}=e^{2\kappa_{+}v}\mbox{ and }V_{\mathcal{H}^{+}}(v)\to 0\mbox{ as }v\to-\infty; (5.6)
d​V𝒞​ℋ+d​v=e−2​κ−​v​ and ​V𝒞​ℋ+​(v)→1​ as ​v→+∞.\frac{dV_{\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}}}{dv}=e^{-2\kappa_{-}v}\mbox{ and }V_{\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}}(v)\to 1\mbox{ as }v\to+\infty. (5.7)

In the (Uℋ+,Vℋ+)(U_{\mathcal{H}^{+}},V_{\mathcal{H}^{+}}) coordinate system, we attach the boundaries ℋ1+:={Uℋ+=0}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}:=\{U_{\mathcal{H}^{+}}=0\} and ℋ2+:={Vℋ+=0}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2}:=\{V_{\mathcal{H}^{+}}=0\}. Denote also the event horizon as ℋt​o​t​a​l+=ℋ1+∪ℋ2+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{total}=\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}\cup\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2}. In the (U𝒞​ℋ+,V𝒞​ℋ+)(U_{\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}},V_{\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}}) coordinate system, we attach the boundaries 𝒞ℋ1+:={V𝒞​ℋ+=1}\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}:=\{V_{\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}}=1\} and 𝒞ℋ2+:={U𝒞​ℋ+=1}\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2}:=\{U_{\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}}=1\}. Denote also the Cauchy horizon as 𝒞​ℋt​o​t​a​l+=𝒞​ℋ1+∪𝒞​ℋ2+\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{total}=\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}\cup\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2}. Notice that in our convention, the bifurcation sphere of ℋt​o​t​a​l+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{total}, which is given by {(Uℋ+,Vℋ+):Uℋ+=Vℋ+=0}\{(U_{\mathcal{H}^{+}},V_{\mathcal{H}^{+}}):U_{\mathcal{H}^{+}}=V_{\mathcal{H}^{+}}=0\} belongs to both ℋ1+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1} and ℋ2+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2} (in fact, it is precisely ℋ1+∩ℋ2+\mathcal{H}_{1}^{+}\cap\mathcal{H}_{2}^{+}). Similarly for the the bifurcation sphere of 𝒞​ℋt​o​t​a​l+\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{total}. Notice that the metric extends smoothly to the boundaries. We refer the reader to the shaded region of Figure 1 for a depiction of these boundaries.

5.1.3. The (U,v)(U,v) coordinate system

Here and in Section 5.1.4, we will compute the metric in two more systems of null coordinates. In particular, these coordinate systems will be regular near ℋ1+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1} and 𝒞​ℋ1+\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1} respectively. In view of the fact that Theorems 5.1 and 5.4 are stated and proved in the neighbourhood of one componenent of the event horizon and one component of the Cauchy horizon, without loss of generality, we will consider a neighbourhood of ℋ1+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1} and 𝒞​ℋ1+\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}. In particular, it will be convenient to introduce the convention that ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+} and 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+} (without subscripts) refer to ℋ1+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1} and 𝒞​ℋ1+\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1} respectively and that U=Uℋ+U=U_{\mathcal{H}^{+}} and V=V𝒞​ℋ+V=V_{\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}}. We will often abuse terminology to also call ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+} and 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+} the event horizon and the Cauchy horizon respectively.

Using the above convention, U=Uℋ+U=U_{\mathcal{H}^{+}} is given by (5.4), i.e.,

d​Ud​u=e2​κ+​u​ and ​U​(u)→0​ as ​u→−∞.\frac{dU}{du}=e^{2\kappa_{+}u}\mbox{ and }\,U(u)\to 0\mbox{ as }u\to-\infty. (5.8)

To distinguish the metric in this coordinate system to that in the (u,v)(u,v) coordinate, we use an extra index ℋ\mathcal{H}. The metric in the coordinate system (U,v)(U,v) takes the form

gR​N,ℋ=−ΩR​N,ℋ22​(d​U⊗d​v+d​v⊗d​U)+rR​N2​d​σ𝕊2,g_{RN,\mathcal{H}}=-\frac{\Omega_{RN,\mathcal{H}}^{2}}{2}(dU\otimes dv+dv\otimes dU)+r_{RN}^{2}d\sigma_{\mathbb{S}^{2}},

where

ΩR​N,ℋ2=−42​κ+​(1−2​MrR​N+𝐞2rR​N2)​U−1.\Omega_{RN,\mathcal{H}}^{2}=-\frac{4}{2\kappa_{+}}\left(1-\frac{2M}{r_{RN}}+\frac{{\bf e}^{2}}{r_{RN}^{2}}\right)U^{-1}.

Notice that for every fixed vv, limU→0ΩR​N,ℋ2​(U,v)\lim_{U\to 0}\Omega_{RN,\mathcal{H}}^{2}(U,v) is non-zero, i.e., (U,v)(U,v) is a regular coordinate system near the event horizon. In fact, we have

limU→0ΩR​N,ℋ2​(U,v)=4​e−2​κ+​r+​(r+−r−)1+κ+κ−r+2​e2​κ+​v.\lim_{U\to 0}\Omega_{RN,\mathcal{H}}^{2}(U,v)=\frac{4e^{-2\kappa_{+}r_{+}}(r_{+}-r_{-})^{1+\frac{\kappa_{+}}{\kappa_{-}}}}{r_{+}^{2}}e^{2\kappa_{+}v}.

Moreover, for every r0∈(r−,r+)r_{0}\in(r_{-},r_{+}), we have the following estimates if rR​N​(U,v)∈[r0,r+]r_{RN}(U,v)\in[r_{0},r_{+}]:

ΩR​N,ℋ2+|∂UrR​N|≤Cr0,M,𝐞​e2​κ+​v,|∂vrR​N|≤Cr0,M,𝐞​U​e2​κ+​v\Omega_{RN,\mathcal{H}}^{2}+|\partial_{U}r_{RN}|\leq C_{r_{0},M,{\bf e}}e^{2\kappa_{+}v},\quad|\partial_{v}r_{RN}|\leq C_{r_{0},M,{\bf e}}Ue^{2\kappa_{+}v} (5.9)

where Cr0,M,𝐞>0C_{r_{0},M,{\bf e}}>0 is a constant depending only on r0r_{0} and the parameters of the Reissner–Nordström spacetime MM and 𝐞{\bf e}.

5.1.4. The (u,V)(u,V) coordinate system

Finally, we introduce the coordinate system (u,V)(u,V) by defining V=V𝒞​ℋ+V=V_{\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}} as in (5.7), i.e.,

d​Vd​v=e−2​κ−​v​ and ​V​(v)→1​ as ​v→∞.\frac{dV}{dv}=e^{-2\kappa_{-}v}\mbox{ and }V(v)\to 1\mbox{ as }v\to\infty. (5.10)

We use the index 𝒞​ℋ\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H} to denote the metric in this coordinate system, i.e.

gR​N,𝒞​ℋ=−ΩR​N,𝒞​ℋ22​(d​u⊗d​V+d​V⊗d​u)+rR​N2​d​σ𝕊2,g_{RN,\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}}=-\frac{\Omega_{RN,\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}}^{2}}{2}(du\otimes dV+dV\otimes du)+r_{RN}^{2}d\sigma_{\mathbb{S}^{2}},

where

ΩR​N,𝒞​ℋ2=−42​κ−​(1−2​MrR​N+𝐞2rR​N2)​(1−V)−1.\Omega_{RN,\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}}^{2}=-\frac{4}{2\kappa_{-}}\left(1-\frac{2M}{r_{RN}}+\frac{{\bf e}^{2}}{r_{RN}^{2}}\right)(1-V)^{-1}.

In this coordinate system, the 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+} is given by {V=1}\{V=1\}. Notice that in Reissner–Nordström, (u,V)(u,V) is a smooth coordinate system up to the Cauchy horizon.

In the proofs of Theorems 5.1 and 5.5, we will also show that the metric extends continuously to {V=1}\{V=1\} in the (u,V)(u,V) coordinate system. On the other hand, we will of course not show that the metric extends smoothly as in the Reissner–Nordström case - indeed, in view of Theorems 5.4 and 5.7, this is false for a large class of initial data.

5.2. Stability and instability of the Cauchy horizon

We first state the stability theorem (cf. Step 2(b) in Section 1.1), which, except for the precise quantitative rates, was first proven by Dafermos in [14]. The theorem is formulated below in a gauge that is most convenient for deriving estimates in this paper. We will then compare this with an ‘‘equivalent gauge’’4747 47 Here, we say that two null coordinates vv and v′v^{\prime} are equivalent if c0−1<d​vd​v′​(v′)<c0c_{0}^{-1}<\frac{dv}{dv^{\prime}}(v^{\prime})<c_{0} for some c0>0c_{0}>0. in Remark 5.2, which is more convenient for applying Theorem 4.4.

To give the statement of the theorem, we will use three coordinate systems: (u,v)(u,v), (U,v)(U,v) and (u,V)(u,V). They should be thought of as analogues of the corresponding coordinate systems on the Reissner–Nordström spacetime introduced in Sections 5.1.1, 5.1.3 and 5.1.4 respectively.

We will choose our coordinates as follows. First, we pick the coordinate system (U,v)(U,v), where UU and vv are normalized by the gauge conditions (5.11) and (5.13) below. We then define u⁡(U)u(U) and V⁡(v)V(v) which relate to UU and vv according to (5.8) and (5.10) respectively.

Remark 5.2 (Alternative formulation of the gauge condition).

While the gauge condition on the event horizon as in Theorem 5.1 is suitable for proving estimates, it is less convenient to apply the theorem with this gauge condition. For that purpose, we note that one can alternatively consider the gauge condition ∂vr1−μ=1\frac{\partial_{v}r}{1-\mu}=1 on the set C−∞C_{-\infty} (with the conditions on C¯1\underline{C}_{1} remain unchanged). This will be discussed in detail in Proposition B.1 in Appendix B.

Remark 5.3 (Assumptions in Theorem 5.1 always hold in the global setting).

In fact, the assumptions in Theorem 5.1 always hold for C−∞=ℋ1+C_{-\infty}=\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1} (or for ℋ2+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2}, with appropriate changes of uu and vv) with some s>2s>2, and an arbitrary choice of a transversal initial null curve C¯1\underline{C}_{1}. We check this for ℋ1+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}, as ℋ2+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2} is similar.

We first normalize UU by the gauge condition (5.13) on C¯1\underline{C}_{1} (which will later coincide with {(U,v):v=1,U≤U0}\{(U,v):v=1,\,U\leq U_{0}\}). Note that this is possible because the future-admissibility condition in Definition 3.1 guarantees that for any point on ℋ1+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}, rr is decreasing towards the increasing uu direction; see Lemma 80 in Appendix A.

Next, instead of (1), it suffices to verify the conditions in Proposition B.1. Note that

Moreover, by the C1C^{1} regularity of the initial data, (5.14) follows from standard local existence after a suitable translate of vv.

Thus, as pointed out in celebrated work of Dafermos–Rodnianski [18], one has unconditionally that the boundary of the maximal globally hyperbolic development has non-empty 𝒞​ℋ1+\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1} and 𝒞​ℋ2+\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2}.

Theorems 5.1 and 5.4 give a fairly complete picture of nonlinear stability and instability properties of the Cauchy horizon in a region that is perturbative in the sense that it is C0C^{0} close to a Reissner–Nordström spacetime. Our next result combines these results with Theorem 4.1 to extend this picture to a suitable global non-perturbative setting (cf. Step 3(c) in Section 1.1). For simplicity, we formulate the theorem only for 𝒞​ℋ1+\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}; an entirely symmetric statement holds for 𝒞​ℋ2+\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2}.

Theorem 5.5.

Let (ℳ,g,ϕ,F)(\mathcal{M},g,\phi,F) be the maximal globally hyperbolic future development of an admissible Cauchy initial data set (with arbitrary ω0>2\omega_{0}>2, cf. Definition 3.1). In a neighborhood of ℋ1+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1} in the interior of the black hole, consider the null coordinates (u,V)(u,V) characterized by (5.11), (5.6) on ℋ1+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1} for VV, and (5.13), (5.4) for uu. Moreover, if the lower bound (5.15) holds on ℋ1+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}, then for every u∈(−∞,u𝒞​ℋ1+)u\in(-\infty,u_{\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}), the following blow up of ∂Vϕ\partial_{V}\phi and ∂Vr\partial_{V}r hold:

∫01(∂Vϕ)2Ω2​(u,V)​𝑑V=∞,\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}\frac{(\partial_{V}\phi)^{2}}{\Omega^{2}}(u,V)dV=\infty, (5.18)
limV→1∂VrΩ2​(u,V)=−∞.\displaystyle\lim_{V\to 1}\frac{\partial_{V}r}{\Omega^{2}}(u,V)=-\infty. (5.19)

In particular, the scalar field is not in Wl​o​c1,2W^{1,2}_{loc} and the metric is not in C1C^{1} in the above C0C^{0} extension obtained by adjoining {(u,V):−∞<u<u𝒞​ℋ1+,V=1}\{(u,V):-\infty<u<u_{\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}},V=1\}.

Remark 5.6.

According to Theorem 4.1, if 𝒮=∅\mathcal{S}=\emptyset then 𝒞​ℋ1+∩𝒞​ℋ2+\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}\cap\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2} consists of a bifurcation sphere with positive area radius. In this case, the metric components and the scalar field extend continuously in the (U𝒞​ℋ2+,V𝒞​ℋ1+)(U_{\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2}},V_{\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}) coordinates to the bifurcate sphere (U𝒞​ℋ2+,V𝒞​ℋ1+)=(1,1)(U_{\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2}},V_{\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}})=(1,1), where V𝒞​ℋ1+V_{\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}} coincides with VV in Theorem 5.5 and U𝒞​ℋ2+U_{\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2}} is defined analogously to VV but with respect to ℋ2+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2}, i.e., vv in (5.11) is replaced by uu, and (5.7) is replaced by (5.5). We refer to Remark 10.6 for a proof.

5.3. C2C^{2}-future-inextendibility

The inextendibility statement for the interior region in Theorem 5.5 depends on the particular C0C^{0} extension in the (u,V)(u,V) coordinates. Our final result asserts a geometric formulation of inextendibility of the whole maximal globally hyperbolic future development, namely C2C^{2}-future-inextendibility, which is independent of such a choice (cf. Step 5 in Section 1.1). Notice that since by Remark 5.3, the assumptions in Theorem 5.1 always hold with s>2s>2 when considering the maximal globally hyperbolic future development, we do not need to state those assumptions explicitly in Theorem 5.7.

Theorem 5.7.

Let (ℳ,g,ϕ,F)(\mathcal{M},g,\phi,F) be the maximal globally hyperbolic future development of an admissible Cauchy initial data set (with arbitrary ω0>2\omega_{0}>2, cf. Definition 3.1). Assume furthermore that the lower bound (5.15) holds on ℋ1+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}, as well as on ℋ2+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2} (with vv replaced by uu). Then (ℳ,g)(\mathcal{M},g) is future-inextendible with a C2C^{2} Lorentzian metric.

6. Main theorems for the exterior region proven in [36]

We now discuss the main results for the exterior region, which correspond to Steps 3(a) and 4 in Section 1.1. All of the results in this section are proven in our companion paper [36].

In all the results in this section, the quantities 𝔏(ω0)​0\mathfrak{L}_{(\omega_{0})0}, 𝔏\mathfrak{L} and 𝔏(ω0)​∞\mathfrak{L}_{(\omega_{0})\infty} play an important role. All statements in this section concerning 𝔏(ω0)​0\mathfrak{L}_{(\omega_{0})0}, 𝔏\mathfrak{L} and 𝔏(ω0)​∞\mathfrak{L}_{(\omega_{0})\infty} on one asymptotically flat end applies equally well to 𝔏(ω0)​0′\mathfrak{L}^{\prime}_{(\omega_{0})0}, 𝔏′\mathfrak{L}^{\prime} and 𝔏(ω0)​∞′\mathfrak{L}^{\prime}_{(\omega_{0})\infty} (respectively) on the other asymptotically flat end. We focus on the first asymptotically flat end (i.e., towards which vv and −u-u increase) for the sake of concreteness.

Our first main theorem states that nonvanishing of 𝔏(ω0)​∞\mathfrak{L}_{(\omega_{0})\infty} implies some integrated lower bound for the incoming radiation ∂vϕ\partial_{v}\phi along ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+}.

for every α>min⁡{2​ω0+1,7}\alpha>\min\{2\omega_{0}+1,7\}.
