7. Proof of strong cosmic censorship (Theorem 3.14, Theorem 3.18 and Corollary 3.21)

Combining the results in Sections 4, 5 and 6, we now give the proof of strong cosmic censorship. We first prove the main strong cosmic censorship theorem, which holds for ω0≥3\omega_{0}\geq 3.

Proof of Theorem 3.14.

Step 1. The inextendibility assertion (first statement) follows from Theorems 5.7 and 6.1 (suitably applied to both asymptotically flat ends).

Step 2. The openness assertion (second statement) follows from Theorem 6.2 (where we take ω0\omega_{0} to be the smaller number among ω0\omega_{0} and ω\omega in Theorem 3.14.(2)) applied to both asymptotically flat ends. Indeed, Theorems 6.2 implies that 𝔏\mathfrak{L} and 𝔏′\mathfrak{L}^{\prime} are stable, while by assumption 𝔏(ω0)​0\mathfrak{L}_{(\omega_{0})0} and 𝔏(ω0)​0′\mathfrak{L}_{(\omega_{0})0}^{\prime} are only allowed to be modified by a small perturbation, hence (recalling (3.7)) 𝔏(ω0)​∞\mathfrak{L}_{(\omega_{0})\infty} and 𝔏(ω0)​∞′\mathfrak{L}_{(\omega_{0})\infty}^{\prime} are also stable.

Step 3. The density assertion (third statement) is a mere restatement of Theorem 6.3 applied to both asymptotically flat ends. ∎

Next, we turn to the case where ω0∈(2,3)\omega_{0}\in(2,3).

Sketch of proof of Theorem 3.18.

This is much simpler than the proof of Theorem 3.14 since for ω0∈(2,3)\omega_{0}\in(2,3), 𝔏(ω0)​∞\mathfrak{L}_{(\omega_{0})\infty} and 𝔏(ω0)​∞′\mathfrak{L}^{\prime}_{(\omega_{0})\infty} are not dynamical, i.e., 𝔏(ω0)​∞=𝔏(ω0)​0\mathfrak{L}_{(\omega_{0})\infty}=\mathfrak{L}_{(\omega_{0})0}, 𝔏(ω0)​∞′=𝔏(ω0)​0′\mathfrak{L}^{\prime}_{(\omega_{0})\infty}=\mathfrak{L}^{\prime}_{(\omega_{0})0} can be computed from initial data alone.

The inextendibility assertion again follows immediately from Theorems 5.7 and 6.1. The openness assertion is obvious, in view of the fact 𝔏(ω0)​∞=𝔏(ω0)​0\mathfrak{L}_{(\omega_{0})\infty}=\mathfrak{L}_{(\omega_{0})0}, 𝔏(ω0)​∞′=𝔏(ω0)​0′\mathfrak{L}^{\prime}_{(\omega_{0})\infty}=\mathfrak{L}^{\prime}_{(\omega_{0})0}. Finally, for the density assertion, say, for 𝔏(ω0)​0\mathfrak{L}_{(\omega_{0})0}, it suffices to construct a one-parameter family of initial data such that the incoming part ∂u(rϕ)=−∂ρ(rϕ)+frϕ˙+f​ℓ​ϕr\partial_{u}(r\phi)=-\partial_{\rho}(r\phi)+fr\dot{\phi}+\frac{f\ell\phi}{r} (cf. Lemma 2.3) has an ϵ​ρ−ω0\epsilon\rho^{-\omega_{0}} tail as ρ→∞\rho\to\infty. Such a one-parameter family of initial data (satisfying constraint) is easily seen to exist if one follows the ideas for solving the constraint equations in the proof of Theorem 6.3 in [36]. We omit the details. ∎

Finally, we prove the instability of both the future and past smooth Cauchy horizons of Reissner–Nordström.

Proof of Corollary 3.21.

Given i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N}, we construct Θi\Theta_{i} as follows. By Theorem 6.3 (and considerations in Remark 3.17), one can perturb a future-admissible hypersurface Σ0\Sigma_{0} (i.e., one on which the induced data are future-admissible) in Reissner–Nordström to obtain a perturbation Θ~i∈∩ω>2(𝒜ℐ𝒟(ω)∩Cω∞)\tilde{\Theta}_{i}\in\cap_{\omega>2}(\mathcal{A}\mathcal{I}\mathcal{D}(\omega)\cap C^{\infty}_{\omega}) with compactly supported scalar field such that d3​(Θ~i,ΘR​N,M,𝐞)<2−id_{3}(\tilde{\Theta}_{i},\Theta_{RN,M,{\bf e}})<2^{-i} and 𝔏(3)​∞​[Θ~i]≠0\mathfrak{L}_{(3)\infty}[\tilde{\Theta}_{i}]\neq 0 and 𝔏(3)​∞′​[Θ~i]≠0\mathfrak{L}_{(3)\infty}^{\prime}[\tilde{\Theta}_{i}]\neq 0. If the maximal globally hyperbolic future-and-past development is C2C^{2}-past-extendible, we take Θi=Θ~i\Theta_{i}=\tilde{\Theta}_{i}. Otherwise, one can, by Cauchy stability, solve towards the past to obtain a past-admissible Cauchy data set. Both the openness and density assertions in Theorem 3.14 and Cauchy stability imply the existence of a Θi∈∩ω>2(𝒜ℐ𝒟(ω)∩Cω∞)\Theta_{i}\in\cap_{\omega>2}(\mathcal{A}\mathcal{I}\mathcal{D}(\omega)\cap C^{\infty}_{\omega}), again with compactly supported scalar field, such that

  • •

    on Σ0\Sigma_{0}, d3​(Θi,Θ~i)<2−id_{3}(\Theta_{i},\tilde{\Theta}_{i})<2^{-i},

  • •

    𝔏(3)​∞​[Θi]≠0\mathfrak{L}_{(3)\infty}[{\Theta}_{i}]\neq 0 and 𝔏(3)​∞′​[Θi]≠0\mathfrak{L}_{(3)\infty}^{\prime}[{\Theta}_{i}]\neq 0

  • •

    the maximal globally hyperbolic future-and-past development arising from Θi\Theta_{i} is C2C^{2}-future-and-past-inextendible.

We now show that the sequence (Θi)i∈ℕ(\Theta_{i})_{i\in\mathbb{N}} satisfies the desired properties.

  • •

    Assertion 1: Θi∈∩ω>2(𝒜ℐ𝒟(ω)∩Cω∞)\Theta_{i}\in\cap_{\omega>2}(\mathcal{A}\mathcal{I}\mathcal{D}(\omega)\cap C^{\infty}_{\omega}) for all i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N}. This holds by construction.

  • •

    Assertion 2: Compact support of initial scalar field. Note that the final assertion in Theorem 6.3 (when suitably applied to both asymptotically flat ends) implies that the support of the perturbations of ϕ\phi and ϕ˙\dot{\phi} is contained in a fixed large interval [−ρ2¯,ρ¯2][-\bar{\rho_{2}},\bar{\rho}_{2}]. Since the scalar field vanishes on Reissner–Nordström, the assertion follows.

  • •

    Assertion 3: Θi→ΘR​N,M,𝐞\Theta_{i}\to\Theta_{RN,M,{\bf e}} as i→∞i\to\infty with respect to the metric dωd_{\omega}. For ω=3\omega=3, it follows from the construction (and triangle inequality) that d3​(Θi,ΘR​N,M,𝐞)<2−i+1→0d_{3}(\Theta_{i},\Theta_{RN,M,{\bf e}})<2^{-i+1}\to 0. That this also holds for all ω>3\omega>3 follows from the (uniform) compact support of the scalar field.

  • •

    Assertion 4: Existence of future-and-past bifurcate Cauchy horizons. This is proven in [15].

  • •

    Assertion 5: Future-and-past inextendibility. This holds by construction. ∎

This concludes the proof of strong cosmic censorship, assuming the results in Sections 5 and 6. The remainder of this paper will be devoted to the proofs of the theorems in Sections 5.

8. Stability of the Cauchy horizon: Proof of Theorem 5.1

In this section, we carry out the proof of Theorem 5.1. First, we begin with a brief discussion on the ideas of the proof in Section 8.1. We then introduce the quantity Ψ\Psi that we will bound in Section 8.2. In the same section, we derive the bounds for the metric components on the initial hypersurface. Then, in Section 8.3, we will discuss the strategy of the proof, in which we will in particular introduce a partition of the spacetime into the red-shift and blue-shift regions5454 54 We comment on the nomenclature of these regions. The naming of the regions as the red-shift and blue-shift regions originates in [12, 14]. In these works, Dafermos estimated the gauge invariant derivatives of ϕ\phi including ∂uϕ∂ur\frac{\partial_{u}\phi}{\partial_{u}r} and ∂vϕ∂vr\frac{\partial_{v}\phi}{\partial_{v}r} and these quantities tend to decay or grow in the red-shift or blue-shift region respectively. In the present work, since we bound coordinate derivatives of the scalar field, such growth or decay is not manifest. Nevertheless, it should be noted that our choice of the norms is inspired in part by the red-shift/blue-shift estimates in [12, 14].. We will then derive estimates for Ψ\Psi separately in the red-shift and blue-shift regions in Sections 8.4 and 8.5 respectively. We will then prove the C0C^{0} stability statement in Section 8.6 and conclude the proof of Theorem 5.1. Finally, we end with Section 8.7 in which we prove some additional estimates for ∂vr\partial_{v}r which will be used in the proof of the instability theorem.

8.1. Ideas of the proof

Our proof is strongly inspired by the recent work [16] on the stability of the Kerr Cauchy horizon. More precisely, it is based on the following ideas:

  1. (1)

    We view the problem as a stability problem and control only the quantities that remain close to the background Reissner–Nordström spacetime. We bound the difference of these quantities with their background Reissner–Nordström value and call these differences Ψ\Psi. These quantities include the scalar field, the metric components, as well as their appropriately weighted derivatives5555 55 Notice that we control for instance ∂vΨ\partial_{v}\Psi, but ∂v\partial_{v} is in fact a degenerate derivative near the Cauchy horizon.. In particular, unlike in [14], no estimates are derived for the Hawking mass, which according to [14] blows up for a large subclass of initial data.

  2. (2)

    In spherical symmetry, instead of working in L2L^{2} based spaces as in [16], one can directly control Ψ\Psi and its derivatives in L∞L^{\infty} with weights in uu and vv. The key is to prove estimates for Ψ\Psi and its derivatives which are weighted in |u|s|u|^{s} or vsv^{s} with no loss in the polynomial power ss compared to initial data. To this end, we first observe that the background values of5656 56 See definitions in Sections 2 and 5.1. Ω\Omega, ∂ur\partial_{u}r and ∂vr\partial_{v}r in the (u,v)(u,v) coordinate system are exponential functions in u+vu+v and one can use basic calculus facts such as Lemmas 8.4 and 8.8 to ensure that the estimates for ∂uΨ\partial_{u}\Psi and ∂vΨ\partial_{v}\Psi do not lose in the polynomial weights. For Ψ\Psi itself, we will bound a degenerate quantity e−κ−​(u+v)​Ψe^{-\kappa_{-}(u+v)}\Psi in order to to ensure that we have no loss in the polynomial weight.

  3. (3)

    Finally, we point out the source of smallness that we can exploit in this problem. By restricting ourselves to the future development of C¯1′∪C−∞\underline{C}^{\prime}_{1}\cup C_{-\infty}, we create a smallness parameter which is sufficient to deal with all terms that are nonlinear in Ψ\Psi. On the other hand, to deal with the linear terms, we face the problem that we need to prove estimates in a “large” region of spacetime and this largeness is reflected by the fact that the rr difference between two points in this region need not be small. To handle this, we divide the spacetime into finitely many regions each of which has small rr difference. This is a way of exploiting the linearity of these terms and can be viewed as a naive substitute of Grönwall’s inequality in this setting with two variables5757 57 A similar idea was exploited to derive the BV estimates for the scalar field in Section 13 of [14]..

8.2. Setup and bounds for the initial data

As mentioned before, we will work with all of the following coordinate systems: (u,v)(u,v), (U,v)(U,v) and (u,V)(u,V). The (U,v)(U,v) coordinates are chosen on the initial hypersurfaces by the gauge conditions (5.11) and (5.13). We then define the uu and VV coordinates by (5.8) and (5.10) respectively.

For any fixed choice of null coordinate system, we write the metric in the form given by (2.1) and (2.2). We will label the metric components5858 58 Notice that the values of rr are independent of the choice of the null coordinates. by (Ωℋ2,r)(\Omega^{2}_{\mathcal{H}},r), (Ω2,r)(\Omega^{2},r) and (Ω𝒞​ℋ2,r)(\Omega^{2}_{\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}},r) in the (U,v)(U,v), (u,v)(u,v) and (u,V)(u,V) coordinate systems respectively.

In the proof of the main theorem, we will estimate the scalar field as well as the difference of the metric components with the corresponding Reissner–Nordström spacetime. We find it convenient to introduce that quantity Ψ\Psi which we will estimate in the proof of Theorem 5.1. In the coordinate system (U,v)(U,v), define

Ψ=[ϕr−rR​Nlog⁡ΩℋΩR​N,ℋ.]\Psi=\begin{bmatrix}\phi\\ r-r_{RN}\\ \log\frac{\Omega_{\mathcal{H}}}{\Omega_{RN,\mathcal{H}}}.\end{bmatrix} (8.1)

Notice that here we have taken the functions rR​Nr_{RN} and ΩR​N,ℋ\Omega_{RN,\mathcal{H}} to be the metric components of a Reissner–Nordström spacetime with parameters MM and 𝐞{\bf e} equal to that in Theorem 5.1. In the (u,v)(u,v) coordinate system, we also define

Ψ=[ϕr−rR​Nlog⁡ΩΩR​N]\Psi=\begin{bmatrix}\phi\\ r-r_{RN}\\ \log\frac{\Omega}{\Omega_{RN}}\end{bmatrix}

We make a similar definition in the (u,V)(u,V) coordinate system.

The functions rr and ϕ\phi are manifestly independent of the choice of the null coordinates. Notice that we also have log⁡ΩℋΩR​N,ℋ=log⁡ΩΩR​N=log⁡Ω𝒞​ℋΩR​N,𝒞​ℋ\log\frac{\Omega_{\mathcal{H}}}{\Omega_{RN,\mathcal{H}}}=\log\frac{\Omega}{\Omega_{RN}}=\log\frac{\Omega_{\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}}}{\Omega_{RN,\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}}}. We will therefore refer to Ψ\Psi without mentioning explicitly which coordinate system we are considering.

To proceed, we further introduce the notation that

|Ψ|2:=|ϕ|2+|r−rR​N|2+|log⁡ΩℋΩR​N,ℋ|2.|\Psi|^{2}:=|\phi|^{2}+|r-r_{RN}|^{2}+\left|\log\frac{\Omega_{\mathcal{H}}}{\Omega_{RN,\mathcal{H}}}\right|^{2}.

We also define |∂vΨ||\partial_{v}\Psi|, |∂VΨ||\partial_{V}\Psi|, |∂uΨ||\partial_{u}\Psi| and |∂UΨ||\partial_{U}\Psi| in the obvious manner.

Before we end this subsection, we prove some bounds for Ψ\Psi and its derivatives on the initial hypersurfaces. This will be the starting point of the later subsections in which we bound Ψ\Psi in the spacetime solution.

Proposition 8.1.

Under the assumptions of Theorem 5.1, there exists constant D=D⁡(M,𝐞,s,E)>0D=D(M,{\bf e},s,E)>0 such that on {U=0}\{U=0\}, we have

|Ψ|​(0,v)+|∂vΨ|​(0,v)≤D​v−s;|\Psi|(0,v)+|\partial_{v}\Psi|(0,v)\leq Dv^{-s}; (8.2)

and on {v=1}\{v=1\}, we have

|∂UΨ|​(U,0)≤D.|\partial_{U}\Psi|(U,0)\leq D. (8.3)

Moreover, by choosing D=D⁡(M,𝐞,s,E)>0D=D(M,{\bf e},s,E)>0 larger if necessary, we have the additional estimate on {U=0}\{U=0\},

|∂UΨ|​(0,v)≤D​e2​κ+​v​v−s;|\partial_{U}\Psi|(0,v)\leq De^{2\kappa_{+}v}v^{-s}; (8.4)

and on {v=1}\{v=1\}, we also have

|Ψ|​(U,1)+|∂vΨ|​(U,1)≤D.|\Psi|(U,1)+|\partial_{v}\Psi|(U,1)\leq D. (8.5)
Proof.

On {U=0}\{U=0\}, we recall the gauge condition (5.11):

Hence, by definition, for Ωℋ\Omega_{\mathcal{H}} in the (U,v)(U,v) coordinate system, we have

(log⁡Ωℋ−log⁡ΩR​N,ℋ)​(0,v)=0.\left(\log\Omega_{\mathcal{H}}-\log\Omega_{RN,\mathcal{H}}\right)(0,v)=0. (8.6)

Since ∂vϕ\partial_{v}\phi is given, rr can be computed by (2.4), namely

∂v(e−2​κ+​v​∂vr)=−e−2​κ+​v​r​(∂vϕ)2.\partial_{v}(e^{-2\kappa_{+}v}\partial_{v}r)=-e^{-2\kappa_{+}v}r(\partial_{v}\phi)^{2}.

Integrating this equation from v=1v=1 to v=∞v=\infty, we obtain

limv→∞(e−2​κ+​v​∂vr⁡(0,v)+∫1ve−2​κ+​v′​r​(∂vϕ)2​(0,v′)​d​v′)=e−2​κ+​∂vr⁡(0,1).\lim_{v\to\infty}(e^{-2\kappa_{+}v}\partial_{v}r(0,v)+\int_{1}^{v}e^{-2\kappa_{+}v^{\prime}}r(\partial_{v}\phi)^{2}(0,v^{\prime})\,dv^{\prime})=e^{-2\kappa_{+}}\partial_{v}r(0,1).

We claim that

limv→∞∫1ve−2​κ+​v′​r​(∂vϕ)2​(0,v′)​d​v′=e−2​κ+​∂vr⁡(0,1).\lim_{v\to\infty}\int_{1}^{v}e^{-2\kappa_{+}v^{\prime}}r(\partial_{v}\phi)^{2}(0,v^{\prime})\,dv^{\prime}=e^{-2\kappa_{+}}\partial_{v}r(0,1).

If not, since we also know that ∂vr⁡(0,v)≥0\partial_{v}r(0,v)\geq 0 (by Lemma 80), it then follows that there exists c>0c>0 so that for vv sufficiently large, ∂vr⁡(0,v)≥c​e2​κ+​v\partial_{v}r(0,v)\geq ce^{2\kappa_{+}v}. This then contradicts the fact that r→M+M2−𝐞2r\to M+\sqrt{M^{2}-{\bf e}^{2}} as v→∞v\to\infty. Now the claim also implies that limv→∞e−2​κ+​v​∂vr⁡(0,v)=0\lim_{v\to\infty}e^{-2\kappa_{+}v}\partial_{v}r(0,v)=0. Therefore, integrating the ∂v(e−2​κ+​v​∂vr)\partial_{v}(e^{-2\kappa_{+}v}\partial_{v}r) equation above, we obtain

|∂vr|​(0,v)≤CM,𝐞,s​𝐞2​v−2​s,|r−rR​N|=|r−(M+M2−𝐞2)|​(0,v)≤CM,𝐞,s​𝐞2​v−2​s+1.|\partial_{v}r|(0,v)\leq C_{M,{\bf e},s}{\bf e}^{2}v^{-2s},\quad|r-r_{RN}|=|r-(M+\sqrt{M^{2}-{\bf e}^{2}})|(0,v)\leq C_{M,{\bf e},s}{\bf e}^{2}v^{-2s+1}. (8.7)

We then note that by the assumptions of Theorem 5.1, ϕ\phi and ∂vϕ\partial_{v}\phi obey the desired estimate. This fact, together with (8.6) and (8.7), prove (8.2).

We turn to the proof of (8.3). On {v=1}\{v=1\}, we set the gauge by the condition ∂Ur=−1.\partial_{U}r=-1. Combined with the bound (5.9) for ∂UrR​N\partial_{U}r_{RN}, (8.3) follows for ∂U(r−rN)\partial_{U}(r-r_{N}). Moreover, by (2.4), we have

∂U(1Ωℋ2)=r​(∂Uϕ)2Ωℋ2,\partial_{U}\left(\frac{1}{\Omega^{2}_{\mathcal{H}}}\right)=\frac{r(\partial_{U}\phi)^{2}}{\Omega_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}},

which implies that for U≤Us≤1U\leq U_{s}\leq 1,

|∂Ulog⁡Ωℋ|​(U,1)≤CM,𝐞​(∂Uϕ)2​(U,1).|\partial_{U}\log\Omega_{\mathcal{H}}|(U,1)\leq C_{M,{\bf e}}(\partial_{U}\phi)^{2}(U,1).

These observations, together with the assumption of Theorem 5.1 on ∂Uϕ\partial_{U}\phi, imply (8.3).

Once we have proven (8.2) and (8.3), it is easy to see that (8.4) and (8.5) follow directly from integration and the use of the equations (2.3). ∎

8.3. Strategy of the proof

From this point onwards, we work under the assumptions of Theorem 5.1. In order to prove Theorem 5.1, we will estimate Ψ\Psi (as defined in (8.1)) and its derivatives. Since we are allowed to restrict to the future development of a subset C¯1′\underline{C}_{1}^{\prime} of C¯1\underline{C}_{1}, we only need to prove the bounds in 0≤U≤Us0\leq U\leq U_{s} for some UsU_{s} sufficiently small (or equivalently −∞<u≤us-\infty<u\leq u_{s} for some usu_{s} sufficiently negative). These estimates will be proven in the following two steps:

  1. (1)

    First, we prove estimates in a neighborhood of the event horizon, {(u,v):v≥1,u+v≤A1}\{(u,v):v\geq 1,\,u+v\leq A_{1}\} for A1A_{1} sufficiently negative. This will be called the red-shift region ℛ\mathcal{R}. The choice of A1A_{1} depends on the size of the initial data (in particular on DD in Proposition 8.1).

  2. (2)

    Second, after A1A_{1} is fixed, we further divide the remaining region. Define ℬi:={(u,v):Ai≤u+v<Ai+1,u≤ui}\mathcal{B}_{i}:=\{(u,v):A_{i}\leq u+v<A_{i+1},u\leq u_{i}\} for i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n, where A1<A2<⋯<An<An+1:=∞A_{1}<A_{2}<\dots<A_{n}<A_{n+1}:=\infty, u1>u2>⋯>unu_{1}>u_{2}>\dots>u_{n} (all of these parameters will be chosen in the course of the proof). The choice of AiA_{i} depends only on A1A_{1}, the parameters of the background Reissner–Nordström spacetime MM, 𝐞{\bf e}, and also ss. In particular it does not depend explicitly on the size of the data. We then show that as long as uiu_{i} is sufficient negative and ui≤ui−1u_{i}\leq u_{i-1} (in a way that can depend on the size of the data), one can obtain good estimates for the solution in each of these regions. Finally, choosing us≤unu_{s}\leq u_{n}, we conclude the proof of the main theorem.

    We will call ℬ:=(∪i=1nℬi)∩{(u,v):u≤us}\mathcal{B}:=(\cup_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{B}_{i})\cap\{(u,v):u\leq u_{s}\} the blue-shift region.

A depiction of the partition of the spacetime and the various parameters involved is given in Figure 6.

We will carry out the estimates in the two steps above in the next two subsections. We then combine these bounds and conclude the proof of the main theorem in Section 8.6.

8.4. The red-shift region

In this subsection, we work with the (U,v)(U,v) coordinate system since it is regular in the red-shift region. Define the red-shift region as follows:

ℛ:={(U,v):Ue2​κ+​v≤δ,v≥1,U≥0},\mathcal{R}:=\{(U,v):Ue^{2\kappa_{+}v}\leq\delta,\,v\geq 1,\,U\geq 0\},

where δ>0\delta>0 is a small constant to be chosen later. Moreover, as we will show later, the choice of δ\delta depends only on MM, 𝐞{\bf e}, ss and DD. Notice that this definition of ℛ\mathcal{R} is the same as that in Section 8.3 if A1:=12​κ+​log⁡(2​κ+​δ)A_{1}:=\frac{1}{2\kappa_{+}}\log(2\kappa_{+}\delta).

We proceed by writing down a schematic wave equation Ψ\Psi under certain bootstrap assumptions. Assume that the following bound holds throughout ℛ\mathcal{R}:

|Ψ|≤4​D.|\Psi|\leq 4D. (8.8)

We also need the following bootstrap assumptions:

|log⁡Ωℋ−log⁡ΩR​N,ℋ|≤1100,|\log\Omega_{\mathcal{H}}-\log\Omega_{RN,\mathcal{H}}|\leq\frac{1}{100}, (8.9)

and

|∂UΨ|​(u,v)≤Δ​e2​κ+​v​v−s,|\partial_{U}\Psi|(u,v)\leq\Delta e^{2\kappa_{+}v}v^{-s}, (8.10)

where Δ\Delta is a large constant to be chosen later.

Subtracting the equations for the Reissner–Nordström solution from that for (ℳ,g,ϕ,F)(\mathcal{M},g,\phi,F) and using (8.8), we obtain

|∂U∂vΨ|≤CM,𝐞,s,D​(e2​κ+​v​(|∂vΨ|+|Ψ|)+|U|​e2​κ+​v​|∂UΨ|+|∂UΨ​∂vΨ|),|\partial_{U}\partial_{v}\Psi|\leq C_{M,{\bf e},s,D}\left(e^{2\kappa_{+}v}(|\partial_{v}\Psi|+|\Psi|)+|U|e^{2\kappa_{+}v}|\partial_{U}\Psi|+|\partial_{U}\Psi\partial_{v}\Psi|\right), (8.11)

where CM,𝐞,s,DC_{M,{\bf e},s,D} is a constant depending only on MM, 𝐞{\bf e}, ss and DD. Notice that in the above we have used the estimates (5.9) on Reissner–Nordström spacetime and also the bound

Ωℋ2−ΩR​N,ℋ2ΩR​N,ℋ2≤C⁡(log⁡Ωℋ−log⁡ΩR​N,ℋ)\frac{\Omega^{2}_{\mathcal{H}}-\Omega^{2}_{RN,\mathcal{H}}}{\Omega^{2}_{RN,\mathcal{H}}}\leq C\left(\log\Omega_{\mathcal{H}}-\log\Omega_{RN,\mathcal{H}}\right) (8.12)

which holds under the bootstrap assumption (8.9).

Our goal in the remainder of this subsection is to use the equation (8.11) to obtain estimates for Ψ\Psi, ∂vΨ\partial_{v}\Psi and ∂uΨ\partial_{u}\Psi. In particular, we will recover the bootstrap assumptions (8.8), (8.9) and (8.10). We can immediately observe that in fact we can obtain a bound for Ψ\Psi using (8.10). In particular, since v≥1v\geq 1, the estimate in the following proposition improves the bootstrap assumptions (8.8) and (8.9):

Proposition 8.2.

Under the bootstrap assumptions (8.8), (8.9) and (8.10), for δ=δ⁡(Δ,D)>0\delta=\delta(\Delta,D)>0 sufficiently small, the following estimates hold for (U,v)∈ℛ(U,v)\in\mathcal{R}:

|Ψ|​(U,v)≤2​D​v−s|\Psi|(U,v)\leq 2Dv^{-s}

and

|log⁡Ωℋ−log⁡ΩR​N,ℋ|​(U,v)≤1200.|\log\Omega_{\mathcal{H}}-\log\Omega_{RN,\mathcal{H}}|(U,v)\leq\frac{1}{200}.
Proof.

We apply the bound for the initial data in Proposition 8.1, the bootstrap assumption (8.10) and the fact that U​e2​κ+​v≤δUe^{2\kappa_{+}v}\leq\delta to get

|Ψ|​(U,v)≤|Ψ|​(0,v)+∫0U|∂UΨ|​(U′,v)​d​U′≤D​v−s+∫0UΔ​e2​κ+​v​v−s​d​U′≤(D+Δ​δ)​v−s≤2​D​v−s,\begin{split}|\Psi|(U,v)\leq&|\Psi|(0,v)+\int_{0}^{U}|\partial_{U}\Psi|(U^{\prime},v)dU^{\prime}\\ \leq&Dv^{-s}+\int_{0}^{U}\Delta e^{2\kappa_{+}v}v^{-s}\,dU^{\prime}\leq(D+\Delta\delta)v^{-s}\leq 2Dv^{-s},\end{split}

after choosing δ\delta to be sufficiently small. To show the second bound stated in the proposition, notice that by (8.6), log⁡Ωℋ−log⁡ΩR​N,ℋ\log\Omega_{\mathcal{H}}-\log\Omega_{RN,\mathcal{H}} is vanishing for U=0U=0. We can therefore repeat the argument above without the D​v−sDv^{-s} term, i.e., we have

|log⁡Ωℋ−log⁡ΩR​N,ℋ|​(U,v)≤∫0UΔ​e2​κ+​v​v−s​d​U′≤Δ​δ​v−s≤1200|\log\Omega_{\mathcal{H}}-\log\Omega_{RN,\mathcal{H}}|(U,v)\leq\int_{0}^{U}\Delta e^{2\kappa_{+}v}v^{-s}\,dU^{\prime}\leq\Delta\delta v^{-s}\leq\frac{1}{200}

for δ\delta sufficiently small. ∎

Using this we get a bound for ∂vΨ\partial_{v}\Psi:

Proposition 8.3.

Under the bootstrap assumptions (8.8), (8.9) and (8.10), for δ=δ⁡(M,𝐞,Δ,D)>0\delta=\delta(M,{\bf e},\Delta,D)>0 sufficiently small, the following estimate holds for (U,v)∈ℛ(U,v)\in\mathcal{R}:

|∂vΨ|​(U,v)≤2​D​v−s.|\partial_{v}\Psi|(U,v)\leq 2Dv^{-s}.
Proof.

Integrating (8.11) and using Proposition 8.1, the bootstrap assumption (8.10) and Proposition 8.2, we obtain

|∂vΨ|​(U,v)≤|∂vΨ|​(0,v)+∫0U|∂U∂vΨ|​(U′,v)​d​U′≤D​v−s+CM,𝐞,s,D​∫0U(e2​κ+​v​(|∂vΨ|+|Ψ|)+|U′|​e2​κ+​v​|∂UΨ|+|∂UΨ|​|∂vΨ|)​(U′,v)​d​U′≤(D+2​CM,𝐞,s,D​U​e2​κ+​v+CM,𝐞,s,D​Δ​U2​e4​κ+​v)​v−s+CM,𝐞,s,D∫0U(e2​κ+​v+|∂UΨ|(U′,v))|∂vΨ|(U′,v)dU′.\begin{split}&|\partial_{v}\Psi|(U,v)\leq|\partial_{v}\Psi|(0,v)+\int_{0}^{U}|\partial_{U}\partial_{v}\Psi|(U^{\prime},v)dU^{\prime}\\ \leq&Dv^{-s}+C_{M,{\bf e},s,D}\int_{0}^{U}\left(e^{2\kappa_{+}v}(|\partial_{v}\Psi|+|\Psi|)+|U^{\prime}|e^{2\kappa_{+}v}|\partial_{U}\Psi|+|\partial_{U}\Psi||\partial_{v}\Psi|\right)(U^{\prime},v)\,dU^{\prime}\\ \leq&(D+2C_{M,{\bf e},s,D}Ue^{2\kappa_{+}v}+C_{M,{\bf e},s,D}\Delta U^{2}e^{4\kappa_{+}v})v^{-s}\\ &+C_{M,{\bf e},s,D}\int_{0}^{U}\left(e^{2\kappa_{+}v}+|\partial_{U}\Psi|(U^{\prime},v)\right)|\partial_{v}\Psi|(U^{\prime},v)\,dU^{\prime}.\end{split}

Recalling that in the red-shift region U​e2​κ+​v≤δUe^{2\kappa_{+}v}\leq\delta, we can thus choose δ\delta to be sufficiently small such that the first term is ≤3​D2​v−s\leq\frac{3D}{2}v^{-s}. We then apply Grönwall’s inequality to get

|∂vΨ|​(U,v)≤3​D2​v−s​eCM,𝐞,s,D​U​e2​κ+​v+CM,𝐞,s,D​∫0U|∂UΨ|​(U′,v)​d​U′≤3​D2​v−s​eCM,𝐞,s,D​δ+CM,𝐞,s,D​Δ​δ​v−s.|\partial_{v}\Psi|(U,v)\leq\frac{3D}{2}v^{-s}e^{C_{M,{\bf e},s,D}Ue^{2\kappa_{+}v}+C_{M,{\bf e},s,D}\int_{0}^{U}|\partial_{U}\Psi|(U^{\prime},v)\,dU^{\prime}}\leq\frac{3D}{2}v^{-s}e^{C_{M,{\bf e},s,D}\delta+C_{M,{\bf e},s,D}\Delta\delta v^{-s}}.

Choosing δ\delta to be sufficiently small depending on MM, 𝐞{\bf e}, DD and Δ\Delta, we thus have obtained the desired conclusion. ∎

Our goal is then to use the above bounds to control ∂UΨ\partial_{U}\Psi and to improve the bootstrap assumption (8.10). Before we proceed to the estimates for ∂UΨ\partial_{U}\Psi, we first prove a simple lemma:

Lemma 8.4.

For every real numbers s≥0s\geq 0 and v≥1v\geq 1, we have

∫1ve2​κ+​v′​(v′)−s​d​v′≤Cκ+,s​e2​κ+​v​v−s,\int_{1}^{v}e^{2\kappa_{+}v^{\prime}}(v^{\prime})^{-s}\,dv^{\prime}\leq C_{\kappa_{+},s}e^{2\kappa_{+}v}v^{-s},

for some Cκ+,s>0C_{\kappa_{+},s}>0 depending only on κ+\kappa_{+} and ss.

Proof.

Integrating by parts twice, we obtain

∫1ve2​κ+​v′​(v′)−s​d​v′≤12​κ+​e2​κ+​v​v−s+s2​κ+​∫1ve2​κ+​v′​(v′)−s−1​d​v′≤12​κ+​e2​κ+​v​v−s+s4​κ+2​e2​κ+​v​v−s−1+s⁡(s+1)4​κ+2​∫1ve2​κ+​v′​(v′)−s−2​d​v′.\begin{split}\int_{1}^{v}e^{2\kappa_{+}v^{\prime}}(v^{\prime})^{-s}\,dv^{\prime}\leq&\frac{1}{2\kappa_{+}}e^{2\kappa_{+}v}v^{-s}+\frac{s}{2\kappa_{+}}\int_{1}^{v}e^{2\kappa_{+}v^{\prime}}(v^{\prime})^{-s-1}\,dv^{\prime}\\ \leq&\frac{1}{2\kappa_{+}}e^{2\kappa_{+}v}v^{-s}+\frac{s}{4\kappa_{+}^{2}}e^{2\kappa_{+}v}v^{-s-1}+\frac{s(s+1)}{4\kappa_{+}^{2}}\int_{1}^{v}e^{2\kappa_{+}v^{\prime}}(v^{\prime})^{-s-2}\,dv^{\prime}.\end{split}

The last term can be bounded by

≤s⁡(s+1)4​κ+2​e2​κ+​v​v−s​∫1v(v′)−2​d​v′≤s⁡(s+1)4​κ+2​e2​κ+​v​v−s.\leq\frac{s(s+1)}{4\kappa_{+}^{2}}e^{2\kappa_{+}v}v^{-s}\int_{1}^{v}(v^{\prime})^{-2}\,dv^{\prime}\leq\frac{s(s+1)}{4\kappa_{+}^{2}}e^{2\kappa_{+}v}v^{-s}.

Combining all the bounds above gives the desired conclusion. ∎

Finally, we use the equation (8.11) and the above lemma to estimate ∂UΨ\partial_{U}\Psi and close the bootstrap assumption (8.10).

Proposition 8.5.

Under the bootstrap assumptions (8.8), (8.9) and (8.10), for δ=δ⁡(M,𝐞,Δ,D)>0\delta=\delta(M,{\bf e},\Delta,D)>0 sufficiently small, the following estimate holds for (U,v)∈ℛ(U,v)\in\mathcal{R}:

|∂UΨ|​(U,v)≤CM,𝐞,s,D​e2​κ+​v​v−s,|\partial_{U}\Psi|(U,v)\leq C_{M,{\bf e},s,D}e^{2\kappa_{+}v}v^{-s},

where CM,𝐞,s,DC_{M,{\bf e},s,D} is a constant depending only on MM, 𝐞{\bf e}, ss and DD.

Proof.

Integrating (8.11) in the vv-direction, applying Proposition 8.1 and using Propositions 8.2 and 8.3 together with Lemma 8.4, we get

|∂UΨ|​(U,v)≤D+CM,𝐞,s,D​∫1v(e2​κ+​v′​(|∂vΨ|+|Ψ|)+|U|​e2​κ+​v​|∂UΨ|+|∂UΨ|​|∂vΨ|)​d​v′≤D+CM,𝐞,s,D​∫1ve2​κ+​v′​(v′)−s​d​v′+CM,𝐞,s,D​∫1v(|U|​e2​κ+​v+|∂vΨ|)​|∂UΨ|​d​v′≤D+CM,𝐞,s,D​e2​κ+​v​v−s+CM,𝐞,s,D​∫1v(|U|​e2​κ+​v+|∂vΨ|)​|∂UΨ|​d​v′.\begin{split}|\partial_{U}\Psi|(U,v)\leq&D+C_{M,{\bf e},s,D}\int_{1}^{v}\left(e^{2\kappa_{+}v^{\prime}}(|\partial_{v}\Psi|+|\Psi|)+|U|e^{2\kappa_{+}v}|\partial_{U}\Psi|+|\partial_{U}\Psi||\partial_{v}\Psi|\right)\,dv^{\prime}\\ \leq&D+C_{M,{\bf e},s,D}\int_{1}^{v}e^{2\kappa_{+}v^{\prime}}(v^{\prime})^{-s}\,dv^{\prime}+C_{M,{\bf e},s,D}\int_{1}^{v}(|U|e^{2\kappa_{+}v}+|\partial_{v}\Psi|)|\partial_{U}\Psi|\,dv^{\prime}\\ \leq&D+C_{M,{\bf e},s,D}e^{2\kappa_{+}v}v^{-s}+C_{M,{\bf e},s,D}\int_{1}^{v}(|U|e^{2\kappa_{+}v}+|\partial_{v}\Psi|)|\partial_{U}\Psi|\,dv^{\prime}.\end{split}

Finally, we apply Grönwall’s inequality to get the desired conclusion. ∎

Choosing Δ>CM,𝐞,s,D\Delta>C_{M,{\bf e},s,D}, we have thus improved the bootstrap assumption (8.10) and completed the proof of the following result:

Theorem 8.6.

There exist constants δ=δ⁡(M,𝐞,s,D)>0\delta=\delta(M,{\bf e},s,D)>0 and CM,𝐞,s,D>0C_{M,{\bf e},s,D}>0 such that the following estimate holds for (U,v)∈ℛ(U,v)\in\mathcal{R}:

|Ψ|​(U,v)+|∂vΨ|(U,v)+e−2​κ+​v​|∂UΨ|​(U,v)≤CM,𝐞,s,D​v−s.|\Psi|(U,v)+|\partial_{v}\Psi|(U,v)+e^{-2\kappa_{+}v}|\partial_{U}\Psi|(U,v)\leq C_{M,{\bf e},s,D}v^{-s}.
Proof.

By (8.2), (8.3), (8.4), (8.5) and (8.6), the bootstrap assumptions (8.8), (8.9) and (8.10) hold on the initial hypersurfaces. We then choose Δ>CM,𝐞,s,D\Delta>C_{M,{\bf e},s,D}, where CM,𝐞,s,DC_{M,{\bf e},s,D} is the constant appearing in the statement of Proposition 8.5. After choosing5959 59 Notice that since the choice of Δ\Delta depends only on MM, 𝐞{\bf e}, ss and DD, we can choose δ\delta to depend only on MM, 𝐞{\bf e}, ss and DD. δ=δ⁡(M,𝐞,s,D)>0\delta=\delta(M,{\bf e},s,D)>0 sufficiently small, Propositions 8.2, 8.3 and 8.5 then imply that the bootstrap assumptions (8.8), (8.9) and (8.10) can in fact be improved and hold with a better constant. A standard continuity argument then shows that the desired estimates hold. ∎

We now fix a δ\delta so that Theorem 8.6 holds.

8.5. The blue-shift region

We now turn to the blue-shift region. In this region, it is convenient to use the (u,v)(u,v) coordinate system. Recall that UU and uu are related by (5.8). The blue-shift region is given in the (u,v)(u,v) coordinates by

ℬ:={(u,v):u+v≥12​κ+log(2κ+δ)=:A1,u≤us,v≥1}.\mathcal{B}:=\{(u,v):u+v\geq\frac{1}{2\kappa_{+}}\log(2\kappa_{+}\delta)=:A_{1},\,u\leq u_{s},\,v\geq 1\}.

As mentioned before, we will define a partition ℬi\mathcal{B}_{i} so that ℬ=(∪i=1nℬi)∩{(u,v):u≤us}\mathcal{B}=(\cup_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{B}_{i})\cap\{(u,v):u\leq u_{s}\}. Given δB>0\delta_{B}>0 (which will be chosen below; see Theorem 8.7) and A1=12​κ+​log⁡(2​κ+​δ)∈(−∞,∞)A_{1}=\frac{1}{2\kappa_{+}}\log(2\kappa_{+}\delta)\in(-\infty,\infty) (which is fixed by Theorem 8.6), define a sequence A1<A2<…<AnA_{1}<A_{2}<...<A_{n} such that

min⁡{e−κ−​Ai−e−κ−​Ai+1,e−2​κ−​Ai−e−2​κ−​Ai+1}=δB.\min\{e^{-\kappa_{-}A_{i}}-e^{-\kappa_{-}A_{i+1}},e^{-2\kappa_{-}A_{i}}-e^{-2\kappa_{-}A_{i+1}}\}=\delta_{B}.

We require nn to be such that

e−2​κ−​An≤δB.e^{-2\kappa_{-}A_{n}}\leq\delta_{B}.

Moreover, we will use the convention that

An+1=∞.A_{n+1}=\infty.

Define now ℬi\mathcal{B}_{i} by

ℬi:={(u,v):Ai≤u+v≤Ai+1,u≤ui,v≥1},\mathcal{B}_{i}:=\{(u,v):A_{i}\leq u+v\leq A_{i+1},\,u\leq u_{i},\,v\geq 1\},

where uiu_{i} is a decreasing sequence to be chosen below (see Theorem 8.7).

We now state the following main estimates of this subsection:

Theorem 8.7.

Consider the following statements

supu+v=Ai,u≤ui,v≥1|u|s​(|∂uΨ|​(u,v)+|∂vΨ​|(u,v)+|​Ψ|​(u,v))≤Bi,\sup_{u+v=A_{i},\,u\leq u_{i},\,v\geq 1}|u|^{s}(|\partial_{u}\Psi|(u,v)+|\partial_{v}\Psi|(u,v)+|\Psi|(u,v))\leq B_{i}, (8.13)

and

sup(u,v)∈ℬi(|u|s​(|∂uΨ|​(u,v)+|e−κ−​(v+u)​Ψ|​(u,v))CLOSEOPEN+(v−Ai)s​|∂vΨ|​(u,v)+|u|s−1​|Ψ|​(u,v))≤CM,𝐞,s,A1​Bi\begin{split}\sup_{(u,v)\in\mathcal{B}_{i}}\Big(|u|^{s}(|\partial_{u}\Psi|(u,v)+|e^{-\kappa_{-}(v+u)}\Psi|(u,v))&\\ +(v-A_{i})^{s}|\partial_{v}\Psi|(u,v)+|u|^{s-1}|\Psi|(u,v)\Big)&\leq C_{M,{\bf e},s,A_{1}}B_{i}\end{split} (8.14)

on the hypersurface {u+v=Ai}\{u+v=A_{i}\} and in the region ℬi\mathcal{B}_{i} respectively.

Then, given A1∈(−∞,∞)A_{1}\in(-\infty,\infty) and Bi≥0B_{i}\geq 0, there exist δB=δB​(M,𝐞,s,A1)>0\delta_{B}=\delta_{B}(M,{\bf e},s,A_{1})>0 sufficiently small6060 60 We emphasize that the choice of δB\delta_{B} is independent of BiB_{i}. and ui=ui​(M,𝐞,s,Bi)u_{i}=u_{i}(M,{\bf e},s,B_{i}) sufficiently negative such that (8.13) implies (8.14) with a constant CM,𝐞,s,A1C_{M,{\bf e},s,A_{1}} depending only on MM, 𝐞{\bf e}, ss and A1A_{1}.

In order to prove the estimates, we make the following bootstrap assumptions:

sup(u,v)∈ℬi|Ψ|(u,v)≤1100\sup_{(u,v)\in\mathcal{B}_{i}}|\Psi|(u,v)\leq\frac{1}{100} (8.15)

and

sup(u,v)∈ℬi|u|s​|∂uΨ|​(u,v)≤2​Bi.\sup_{(u,v)\in\mathcal{B}_{i}}|u|^{s}|\partial_{u}\Psi|(u,v)\leq 2B_{i}. (8.16)

The bound (8.16) obviously holds initially by (8.13). Notice also that by (8.13), (8.15) holds initially on {(u,v):u+v=Ai,u≤ui,v≥1}\{(u,v):u+v=A_{i},\,u\leq u_{i},\,v\geq 1\} if uiu_{i} is chosen to be sufficiently negative.

The equations for Ψ\Psi together with (8.15) imply that

|∂u∂vΨ|≤CM,𝐞,A1​(e−2​κ−​(v+u)​(|Ψ|+|∂vΨ|+|∂uΨ|)+|∂uΨ​∂vΨ|).|\partial_{u}\partial_{v}\Psi|\leq C_{M,{\bf e},A_{1}}\Big(e^{-2\kappa_{-}(v+u)}(|\Psi|+|\partial_{v}\Psi|+|\partial_{u}\Psi|)+|\partial_{u}\Psi\partial_{v}\Psi|\Big). (8.17)

Here, we have used an analogue of (8.12) which holds in this setting due to (8.15).

Our goal is to show that under the bootstrap assumptions (8.15) and (8.16), we can use the equation (8.17) to control Ψ\Psi and its derivatives. Before we proceed to the estimates, we need a calculus lemma, which can be viewed as an analogue of Lemma 8.4 in the blue-shift region:

Lemma 8.8.

For 1≤α≤21\leq\alpha\leq 2 and u≤−1u\leq-1, we have

∫−v+Aiue−α​κ−​(v+u′)​|u′|−s​d​u′≤C​e−α​κ−​Ai​(v−Ai)−s,\int_{-v+A_{i}}^{u}e^{-\alpha\kappa_{-}(v+u^{\prime})}|u^{\prime}|^{-s}\,du^{\prime}\leq Ce^{-\alpha\kappa_{-}A_{i}}(v-A_{i})^{-s},

where the constant CC depends on MM, 𝐞{\bf e} and ss.

Proof.

Integrating by parts, we obtain6161 61 Notice that the boundary term at u′=uu^{\prime}=u has a good sign.

∫−v+Aiue−α​κ−​(v+u′)​|u′|−s​d​u′≤1α​κ−​e−α​κ−​Ai​(v−Ai)−s+sα​κ−​∫−v+Aiue−α​κ−​(v+u′)​|u′|−s−1​d​u′.\begin{split}&\int_{-v+A_{i}}^{u}e^{-\alpha\kappa_{-}(v+u^{\prime})}|u^{\prime}|^{-s}\,du^{\prime}\\ \leq&\frac{1}{\alpha\kappa_{-}}e^{-\alpha\kappa_{-}A_{i}}(v-A_{i})^{-s}+\frac{s}{\alpha\kappa_{-}}\int_{-v+A_{i}}^{u}e^{-\alpha\kappa_{-}(v+u^{\prime})}|u^{\prime}|^{-s-1}\,du^{\prime}.\end{split}

The second term can be treated as an error term as follows6262 62 In the case u≤−v+Ai+sα​κ−​log⁡(v−Ai)u\leq-v+A_{i}+\frac{s}{\alpha\kappa_{-}}\log(v-A_{i}), we can ignore the first integral below and obtain a better bound.:

∫−v+Aiue−α​κ−​(v+u′)​|u′|−s−1​d​u′=∫−v+Ai+sα​κ−​log⁡(v−Ai)ue−α​κ−​(v+u′)​|u′|−s−1​d​u′+∫−v+Ai−v+Ai+sα​κ−​log⁡(v−Ai)e−α​κ−​(v+u′)​|u′|−s−1​d​u′≤1s​e−α​κ−​Ai​(v−Ai)−s​|u|−s+sα​κ−​e−α​κ−​Ai​(v−Ai)−s−1​log⁡(v−Ai).\begin{split}&\int_{-v+A_{i}}^{u}e^{-\alpha\kappa_{-}(v+u^{\prime})}|u^{\prime}|^{-s-1}\,du^{\prime}\\ =&\int_{-v+A_{i}+\frac{s}{\alpha\kappa_{-}}\log(v-A_{i})}^{u}e^{-\alpha\kappa_{-}(v+u^{\prime})}|u^{\prime}|^{-s-1}\,du^{\prime}+\int_{-v+A_{i}}^{-v+A_{i}+\frac{s}{\alpha\kappa_{-}}\log(v-A_{i})}e^{-\alpha\kappa_{-}(v+u^{\prime})}|u^{\prime}|^{-s-1}\,du^{\prime}\\ \leq&\frac{1}{s}e^{-\alpha\kappa_{-}A_{i}}(v-A_{i})^{-s}|u|^{-s}+\frac{s}{\alpha\kappa_{-}}e^{-\alpha\kappa_{-}A_{i}}(v-A_{i})^{-s-1}\log(v-A_{i}).\end{split}

Combining the bounds above and using u+v≥Aiu+v\geq A_{i} give the desired conclusion. ∎

We now turn to the estimates for Ψ\Psi and its derivatives. Using Lemma 8.8, the bootstrap assumption (8.16) immediately implies the following bound on Ψ\Psi:

Proposition 8.9.

Under the bootstrap assumptions (8.15) and (8.16), there exist δB=δB​(M,𝐞,s,A1)>0\delta_{B}=\delta_{B}(M,{\bf e},s,A_{1})>0 sufficiently small and ui=ui​(M,𝐞,s,Bi)u_{i}=u_{i}(M,{\bf e},s,B_{i}) sufficiently negative such that the following estimate holds for (u,v)∈ℬi(u,v)\in\mathcal{B}_{i}:

|e−κ−​(v+u)​Ψ|​(u,v)≤CM,𝐞,s​Bi​e−κ−​Ai​|u|−s.|e^{-\kappa_{-}(v+u)}\Psi|(u,v)\leq C_{M,{\bf e},s}B_{i}e^{-\kappa_{-}A_{i}}|u|^{-s}.
Proof.

Using the bootstrap assumption (8.16) and Lemma 8.8, we first derive the following bound on a weighted integral of |∂uΨ||\partial_{u}\Psi|:

∫−v+Aiue−κ−​(v+u′)​|∂uΨ|​(u′,v)​d​u′≤2​Bi​∫−v+Aiue−κ−​(v+u′)​|u′|−s​d​u′≤CM,𝐞,s​Bi​e−κ−​Ai​(v−Ai)−s≤CM,𝐞,s​Bi​e−κ−​Ai​|u|−s.\begin{split}\int_{-v+A_{i}}^{u}e^{-\kappa_{-}(v+u^{\prime})}|\partial_{u}\Psi|(u^{\prime},v)\,du^{\prime}\leq&2B_{i}\int_{-v+A_{i}}^{u}e^{-\kappa_{-}(v+u^{\prime})}|u^{\prime}|^{-s}\,du^{\prime}\\ \leq&C_{M,{\bf e},s}B_{i}e^{-\kappa_{-}A_{i}}(v-A_{i})^{-s}\leq C_{M,{\bf e},s}B_{i}e^{-\kappa_{-}A_{i}}|u|^{-s}.\end{split} (8.18)

Now, to estimate e−κ−​(v+u)​|Ψ|e^{-\kappa_{-}(v+u)}|\Psi|, notice that

12​∂u(e−κ−​(v+u)​Ψ)2=e−2​κ−​(v+u)​Ψ​∂uΨ−κ−​(e−κ−​(v+u)​Ψ)2.\frac{1}{2}\partial_{u}(e^{-\kappa_{-}(v+u)}\Psi)^{2}=e^{-2\kappa_{-}(v+u)}\Psi\partial_{u}\Psi-\kappa_{-}(e^{-\kappa_{-}(v+u)}\Psi)^{2}.

The second term has a good sign and therefore by integrating along a constant vv curve, we obtain

(e−κ−​(v+u)​Ψ)2​(u,v)≤e−2​κ−​Ai​Bi2​(v−Ai)−2​s+C​∫−v+Aiue−2​κ−​(v+u′)​|Ψ​∂uΨ|​(u′,v)​d​u′.(e^{-\kappa_{-}(v+u)}\Psi)^{2}(u,v)\leq e^{-2\kappa_{-}A_{i}}B_{i}^{2}(v-A_{i})^{-2s}+C\int_{-v+A_{i}}^{u}e^{-2\kappa_{-}(v+u^{\prime})}|\Psi\partial_{u}\Psi|(u^{\prime},v)du^{\prime}.

This implies, after dividing by6363 63 Note that we only apply this division in the case supu′∈[v+Ai,u]e−κ−​(v+u′)​|Ψ|​(u′,v)≥e−κ−​Ai​Bi​(v−Ai)−s\sup_{u^{\prime}\in[v+A_{i},u]}e^{-\kappa_{-}(v+u^{\prime})}|\Psi|(u^{\prime},v)\geq e^{-\kappa_{-}A_{i}}B_{i}(v-A_{i})^{-s} since the estimate is trivial otherwise. supu′∈[v+Ai,u]e−κ−​(v+u′)​|Ψ|​(u′,v)\sup_{u^{\prime}\in[v+A_{i},u]}e^{-\kappa_{-}(v+u^{\prime})}|\Psi|(u^{\prime},v) on both sides, that

e−κ−​(v+u)​|Ψ|​(u,v)≤C​e−κ−​Ai​Bi​|u|−s+C​∫−v+Aiue−κ−​(v+u′)​|∂uΨ⁡(u′,v)|​d​u′.e^{-\kappa_{-}(v+u)}|\Psi|(u,v)\leq Ce^{-\kappa_{-}A_{i}}B_{i}|u|^{-s}+C\int_{-v+A_{i}}^{u}e^{-\kappa_{-}(v+u^{\prime})}|\partial_{u}\Psi(u^{\prime},v)|du^{\prime}. (8.19)

The conclusion follows from combining (8.18) and (8.19). ∎

We then turn to the estimate for ∂vΨ\partial_{v}\Psi:

Proposition 8.10.

Under the bootstrap assumptions (8.15) and (8.16), there exist δB=δB​(M,𝐞,s,A1)>0\delta_{B}=\delta_{B}(M,{\bf e},s,A_{1})>0 sufficiently small and ui=ui​(M,𝐞,s,Bi)u_{i}=u_{i}(M,{\bf e},s,B_{i}) sufficiently negative such that the following estimate holds for (u,v)∈ℬi(u,v)\in\mathcal{B}_{i}:

|∂vΨ|​(u,v)≤CM,𝐞,s,A1​Bi​(v−Ai)−s.|\partial_{v}\Psi|(u,v)\leq C_{M,{\bf e},s,A_{1}}B_{i}(v-A_{i})^{-s}.
Proof.

Integrating the equation (8.17) and using the initial data bound (8.13), we have

Combining the bootstrap assumption (8.16) and Lemma 8.8 with α=2\alpha=2 , we get

∫−v+Aiue−2​κ−​(v+u′)​|∂uΨ|​(u′,v)​d​u′≤CM,𝐞,s​Bi​e−2​κ−​Ai​(v−Ai)−s.\int_{-v+A_{i}}^{u}e^{-2\kappa_{-}(v+u^{\prime})}|\partial_{u}\Psi|(u^{\prime},v)du^{\prime}\leq C_{M,{\bf e},s}B_{i}e^{-2\kappa_{-}A_{i}}(v-A_{i})^{-s}.

Similarly, using the bound in Proposition 8.9 together with Lemma 8.8 with α=1\alpha=1, we obtain

∫−v+Aiue−2​κ−​(v+u′)​|Ψ|​(u′,v)​d​u′≤CM,𝐞,s​Bi​e−2​κ−​Ai​(v−Ai)−s.\int_{-v+A_{i}}^{u}e^{-2\kappa_{-}(v+u^{\prime})}|\Psi|(u^{\prime},v)du^{\prime}\leq C_{M,{\bf e},s}B_{i}e^{-2\kappa_{-}A_{i}}(v-A_{i})^{-s}.

Therefore, we have

|∂vΨ|​(u,v)≤CM,𝐞,s,A1​Bi​(v−Ai)−s+CM,𝐞,A1​∫−v+Aiu(e−2​κ−​(v+u′)​|∂vΨ|+|∂uΨ|​|∂vΨ|)​(u′,v)​d​u′.|\partial_{v}\Psi|(u,v)\leq C_{M,{\bf e},s,A_{1}}B_{i}(v-A_{i})^{-s}+C_{M,{\bf e},A_{1}}\int_{-v+A_{i}}^{u}\big(e^{-2\kappa_{-}(v+u^{\prime})}|\partial_{v}\Psi|+|\partial_{u}\Psi||\partial_{v}\Psi|\big)(u^{\prime},v)du^{\prime}. (8.21)

To conclude, notice that

∫−v+Aiue−2​κ−​(v+u′)​d​u′≤CM,𝐞​(e−2​κi​Ai−e−2​κi​Ai+1)≤CM,𝐞​δB\int_{-v+A_{i}}^{u}e^{-2\kappa_{-}(v+u^{\prime})}du^{\prime}\leq C_{M,{\bf e}}(e^{-2\kappa_{i}A_{i}}-e^{-2\kappa_{i}A_{i+1}})\leq C_{M,{\bf e}}\delta_{B}

and

∫−v+Aiu|∂uΨ|(u′,v)​d​u′≤Cs​Bi​|u|−s+1≤Cs​Bi​|ui|−s+1.\int_{-v+A_{i}}^{u}|\partial_{u}\Psi|(u^{\prime},v)du^{\prime}\leq C_{s}B_{i}|u|^{-s+1}\leq C_{s}B_{i}|u_{i}|^{-s+1}.

Therefore, applying Grönwall’s inequality to (8.21), we obtain

|∂vΨ|​(u,v)≤CM,𝐞,s,A1​Bi​(v−Ai)−s​eCM,𝐞​δB+Cs​Bi​|ui|−s+1≤CM,𝐞,s,A1​Bi​(v−Ai)−s,|\partial_{v}\Psi|(u,v)\leq C_{M,{\bf e},s,A_{1}}B_{i}(v-A_{i})^{-s}e^{C_{M,{\bf e}}\delta_{B}+C_{s}B_{i}|u_{i}|^{-s+1}}\leq C_{M,{\bf e},s,A_{1}}B_{i}(v-A_{i})^{-s},

where in the last inequality, we have chosen δB=δB​(M,𝐞,s)\delta_{B}=\delta_{B}(M,{\bf e},s) to be sufficiently small and ui=ui​(M,𝐞,s,Bi)u_{i}=u_{i}(M,{\bf e},s,B_{i}) to be sufficiently negative such that eCM,𝐞​δB+Cs​Bi​|ui|−s+1≤2e^{C_{M,{\bf e}}\delta_{B}+C_{s}B_{i}|u_{i}|^{-s+1}}\leq 2. ∎

This allows us to estimate ∂uΨ\partial_{u}\Psi and recover the bootstrap assumption (8.16).

Proposition 8.11.

Under the bootstrap assumptions (8.15) and (8.16), there exist δB=δB​(M,𝐞,s,A1)>0\delta_{B}=\delta_{B}(M,{\bf e},s,A_{1})>0 sufficiently small and ui=ui​(M,𝐞,s,Bi)u_{i}=u_{i}(M,{\bf e},s,B_{i}) sufficiently negative such that the following estimate holds in ℬi\mathcal{B}_{i}:

|∂uΨ|​(u,v)≤32​Bi​|u|−s.|\partial_{u}\Psi|(u,v)\leq\frac{3}{2}B_{i}|u|^{-s}.
Proof.

Using (8.17) and the initial data bound (8.13), we have

|∂uΨ|​(u,v)≤|∂uΨ|​(u,−u+Ai)+∫−u+Aiv|∂v∂uΨ|​d​v′≤Bi​|u|−s+CM,𝐞,A1​∫−u+Aiv(e−2​κ−​(v′+u)​(|∂uΨ|+|∂vΨ|+|Ψ|)+|∂uΨ|​|∂vΨ|)​(u,v′)​d​v′.\begin{split}&|\partial_{u}\Psi|(u,v)\leq|\partial_{u}\Psi|(u,-u+A_{i})+\int_{-u+A_{i}}^{v}|\partial_{v}\partial_{u}\Psi|dv^{\prime}\\ \leq&B_{i}|u|^{-s}+C_{M,{\bf e},A_{1}}\int_{-u+A_{i}}^{v}\left(e^{-2\kappa_{-}(v^{\prime}+u)}(|\partial_{u}\Psi|+|\partial_{v}\Psi|+|\Psi|)+|\partial_{u}\Psi||\partial_{v}\Psi|\right)(u,v^{\prime})dv^{\prime}.\end{split} (8.22)

By Propositions 8.9 and 8.10 and u+v≥Aiu+v\geq A_{i}, we have

∫−u+Aiv(e−2​κ−​(v′+u)​(|Ψ|+|∂vΨ|))​(u,v′)​d​v′≤CM,𝐞,s,A1​Bi​|u|−s​∫−u+Aive−2​κ−​(v′+u)​d​v′≤CM,𝐞,s,A1​Bi​δB​|u|−s≤Bi5​|u|−s,\begin{split}&\int_{-u+A_{i}}^{v}\left(e^{-2\kappa_{-}(v^{\prime}+u)}(|\Psi|+|\partial_{v}\Psi|)\right)(u,v^{\prime})dv^{\prime}\\ \leq&C_{M,{\bf e},s,A_{1}}B_{i}|u|^{-s}\int_{-u+A_{i}}^{v}e^{-2\kappa_{-}(v^{\prime}+u)}dv^{\prime}\leq C_{M,{\bf e},s,A_{1}}B_{i}\delta_{B}|u|^{-s}\leq\frac{B_{i}}{5}|u|^{-s},\end{split}

after choosing δB=δB​(M,𝐞,s,A1)\delta_{B}=\delta_{B}(M,{\bf e},s,A_{1}) to be sufficiently small. Returning to (8.22), we get

|∂uΨ|​(u,v)≤6​Bi5​|u|−s+CM,𝐞,A1​∫−u+Aiv(e−2​κ−​(v′+u)​|∂uΨ|+|∂uΨ|​|∂vΨ|)​(u,v′)​d​v′.\begin{split}|\partial_{u}\Psi|(u,v)\leq&\frac{6B_{i}}{5}|u|^{-s}+C_{M,{\bf e},A_{1}}\int_{-u+A_{i}}^{v}\left(e^{-2\kappa_{-}(v^{\prime}+u)}|\partial_{u}\Psi|+|\partial_{u}\Psi||\partial_{v}\Psi|\right)(u,v^{\prime})dv^{\prime}.\end{split} (8.23)

In order to apply Grönwall’s inequality, notice that

∫−u+Aive−2​κ−​(v′+u)​d​v′≤CM,𝐞​δB\int_{-u+A_{i}}^{v}e^{-2\kappa_{-}(v^{\prime}+u)}dv^{\prime}\leq C_{M,{\bf e}}\delta_{B}

and

∫−u+Aiv|∂vΨ|(u,v′)​d​v′≤CM,𝐞,s,A1​Bi​∫−u+Aiv(v′−Ai)−s​d​v′≤CM,𝐞,s,A1​Bi​|ui|−s+1\int_{-u+A_{i}}^{v}|\partial_{v}\Psi|(u,v^{\prime})dv^{\prime}\leq C_{M,{\bf e},s,A_{1}}B_{i}\int_{-u+A_{i}}^{v}(v^{\prime}-A_{i})^{-s}dv^{\prime}\leq C_{M,{\bf e},s,A_{1}}B_{i}|u_{i}|^{-s+1}

where the latter bound is obtained using Proposition 8.10. Substituting these bounds into (8.23), we then obtain

|∂uΨ|​(u,v)≤6​Bi5​|u|−s×eCM,𝐞​δB+CM,𝐞,s,A1​Bi​|ui|−s+1≤3​Bi2​|u|−s,\begin{split}|\partial_{u}\Psi|(u,v)\leq&\frac{6B_{i}}{5}|u|^{-s}\times e^{C_{M,{\bf e}}\delta_{B}+C_{M,{\bf e},s,A_{1}}B_{i}|u_{i}|^{-s+1}}\leq\frac{3B_{i}}{2}|u|^{-s},\end{split}

after choosing δB=δB​(M,𝐞,s,A1)\delta_{B}=\delta_{B}(M,{\bf e},s,A_{1}) to be sufficiently small and ui=ui​(M,𝐞,s,Bi)u_{i}=u_{i}(M,{\bf e},s,B_{i}) to be sufficiently negative. ∎

Now, notice that the bound for Ψ\Psi derived in Proposition 8.9 is not sufficiently strong to improve the bootstrap assumption (8.15). Nonetheless, we also have the following estimate:

Proposition 8.12.

Under the bootstrap assumptions (8.15) and (8.16), there exist δB=δB​(M,𝐞,s,A1)>0\delta_{B}=\delta_{B}(M,{\bf e},s,A_{1})>0 sufficiently small and ui=ui​(M,𝐞,s,Bi)u_{i}=u_{i}(M,{\bf e},s,B_{i}) sufficiently negative such that the following estimate holds in ℬi\mathcal{B}_{i}:

|Ψ|≤Cs​Bi​|u|−s+1.|\Psi|\leq C_{s}B_{i}|u|^{-s+1}.
Proof.

Using the assumption on the data in Theorem 8.7 and the bootstrap assumption (8.16), we have

|Ψ|​(u,v)≤|Ψ|​(−v+Ai,v)+∫−v+Aiu|∂uΨ|​(u′,v)​d​u′≤Bi​(v−Ai)−s+2​Bi​∫−v+Aiud​u′|u′|s≤Cs​Bi​((v−Ai)−s+|u|−s+1).\begin{split}|\Psi|(u,v)\leq&|\Psi|(-v+A_{i},v)+\int_{-v+A_{i}}^{u}|\partial_{u}\Psi|(u^{\prime},v)\,du^{\prime}\\ \leq&B_{i}(v-A_{i})^{-s}+2B_{i}\int_{-v+A_{i}}^{u}\frac{du^{\prime}}{|u^{\prime}|^{s}}\leq C_{s}B_{i}\left((v-A_{i})^{-s}+|u|^{-s+1}\right).\end{split}

Finally, we conclude by noting that v−Ai≥|u|v-A_{i}\geq|u|. ∎

According to Proposition 8.12, we have thus improved the bootstrap assumption (8.15) after choosing uiu_{i} to be sufficiently negative depending on BiB_{i} and ss. Moreover, we have also improved the bootstrap assumption (8.16) in Proposition 8.11. Together with Propositions 8.9 and 8.10, we conclude the proof of Theorem 8.7. Finally, by iterating the estimate in Theorem 8.7, we obtain the following bounds in the region ℬ\mathcal{B}.

Theorem 8.13.

Given the estimates in the red-shift region ℛ\mathcal{R} in Theorem 8.6, there exists us=us​(M,𝐞,s,D)u_{s}=u_{s}(M,{\bf e},s,D) sufficiently negative such that the following estimates hold for (u,v)∈ℬ(u,v)\in\mathcal{B}:

|∂uΨ|​(u,v)≤CM,𝐞,s,D​|u|−s,|Ψ|​(u,v)≤CM,𝐞,s,D​|u|−s+1,|∂vΨ|​(u,v)≤CM,𝐞,s,D​v−s.|\partial_{u}\Psi|(u,v)\leq C_{M,{\bf e},s,D}|u|^{-s},\quad|\Psi|(u,v)\leq C_{M,{\bf e},s,D}|u|^{-s+1},\quad|\partial_{v}\Psi|(u,v)\leq C_{M,{\bf e},s,D}v^{-s}.
Proof.

To prove the estimates, we apply Theorem 8.7. First, notice that according to Theorem 8.7, δB\delta_{B} depends only on MM, 𝐞{\bf e}, ss and A1A_{1}. Therefore, given A1A_{1} (which depends on MM, 𝐞{\bf e}, ss and DD), we can choose δB\delta_{B} and partition the blue-shift region in ℬi\mathcal{B}_{i}. We now repeatedly apply Theorem 8.7 for each of the ℬi\mathcal{B}_{i} to show that the following holds for every ii,

sup(u,v)∈ℬi(|u|s​(|∂uΨ|​(u,v)+|e−κ−​(v+u)​Ψ|​(u,v))CLOSEOPEN+(v−Ai)s​|∂vΨ|​(u,v)+|u|s−1​|Ψ|​(u,v))≤(CM,𝐞,s,A1∗)i​e2​i​κ−​An​CM,𝐞,s,D∗⁣∗,\begin{split}\sup_{(u,v)\in\mathcal{B}_{i}}\Big(|u|^{s}(|\partial_{u}\Psi|(u,v)+|e^{-\kappa_{-}(v+u)}\Psi|(u,v))&\\ +(v-A_{i})^{s}|\partial_{v}\Psi|(u,v)+|u|^{s-1}|\Psi|(u,v)\Big)\leq&\left(C_{M,{\bf e},s,A_{1}}^{*}\right)^{i}e^{2i\kappa_{-}A_{n}}C_{M,{\bf e},s,D}^{**},\end{split} (8.24)

where CM,𝐞,s,A1∗C_{M,{\bf e},s,A_{1}}^{*} is the constant in the conclusion of Theorem 8.7 and CM,𝐞,s,D∗⁣∗C_{M,{\bf e},s,D}^{**} is a constant that exists by the conclusion of Theorem 8.6. From this we can easily obtain the conclusion. First, note that (v−Ai)−s≤CM,𝐞,s,D​v−s(v-A_{i})^{-s}\leq C_{M,{\bf e},s,D}v^{-s}. Finally, we observe that the right hand side of (8.24) can be bounded uniformly by a constant depending on MM, 𝐞{\bf e}, ss and DD. ∎

8.6. C0C^{0} stability and conclusion of proof of Theorem 5.1

The estimates in the previous two subsections already imply that the spacetime remains regular in the region u≤usu\leq u_{s}, v≥1v\geq 1. In this subsection, we will further show that the metric and the scalar field can be extended in C0C^{0} and moreover the solution approaches Reissner–Nordström in C0C^{0} in the sense given by the last statement in Theorem 5.1.

First, we have the following C0C^{0} extendibility statement:

Proposition 8.14.

In the (u,V)(u,V) coordinate system, one can attach the boundary 𝒞ℋ+:={V=1}\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}:=\{V=1\} such that rr, ϕ\phi and log⁡Ω𝒞​ℋ\log\Omega_{\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}} extend continuously to 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}.

Proof.

Since the metric components of Reissner–Nordström rR​Nr_{RN} and log⁡ΩR​N,𝒞​ℋ\log\Omega_{RN,\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}} are smooth up to {V=1}\{V=1\}, it suffices to show that Ψ\Psi is continuous up to {V=1}\{V=1\}.

First, we note that by the conclusions in Theorems 8.6 and 8.13, the following holds in the (u,V)(u,V) coordinate system if u≤usu\leq u_{s}, V≥12V\geq\frac{1}{2}:

|∂uΨ|​(u,V)≤CM,𝐞,s,D​|u|−s,|∂VΨ|​(u,V)≤CM,𝐞,s,D​|1−V|−1​log−s⁡(11−V),|\partial_{u}\Psi|(u,V)\leq C_{M,{\bf e},s,D}|u|^{-s},\quad|\partial_{V}\Psi|(u,V)\leq C_{M,{\bf e},s,D}|1-V|^{-1}\log^{-s}\left(\frac{1}{1-V}\right), (8.25)

Given a sequence ui→uu_{i}\to u and Vi→1V_{i}\to 1, it then suffices to show that Ψ⁡(ui,Vi)\Psi(u_{i},V_{i}) is a Cauchy sequence. Fix ϵ>0\epsilon>0. Notice that there exists NN such that for i,j≥Ni,j\geq N, we have

|Ψ⁡(ui,Vi)−Ψ⁡(uj,Vj)|≤|∫uiuj|∂uΨ|​(u′,Vi)​d​u′|+|∫ViVj|∂VΨ|​(uj,V′)​d​V′|≤CM,𝐞,s,D​(|∫uiuj|u′|−s​d​u′|+|∫ViVj|1−V′|−1​log−s⁡(11−V′)​d​V′|)≤ϵ.\begin{split}&|\Psi(u_{i},V_{i})-\Psi(u_{j},V_{j})|\\ \leq&\left|\int_{u_{i}}^{u_{j}}|\partial_{u}\Psi|(u^{\prime},V_{i})\,du^{\prime}\right|+\left|\int_{V_{i}}^{V_{j}}|\partial_{V}\Psi|(u_{j},V^{\prime})\,dV^{\prime}\right|\\ \leq&C_{M,{\bf e},s,D}\left(\left|\int_{u_{i}}^{u_{j}}|u^{\prime}|^{-s}\,du^{\prime}\right|+\left|\int_{V_{i}}^{V_{j}}|1-V^{\prime}|^{-1}\log^{-s}\left(\frac{1}{1-V^{\prime}}\right)\,dV^{\prime}\right|\right)\leq\epsilon.\end{split}

This is because for s>1s>1, the integrands in both integrals are integrable. ∎

We now have all the ingredients to conclude the proof of Theorem 5.1.

Proof of Theorem 5.1.

By Theorems 8.6 and 8.13 and standard local existence results, the solution remains regular in the region {(u,v):u≤us,v≥1}\{(u,v):u\leq u_{s},\,v\geq 1\} as long as usu_{s} is sufficiently negative. In particular, the spacetime indeed has a Penrose diagram given by Figure 3. The statement on the continuity of the metric and the scalar field up to 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+} is given by Proposition 8.14. Finally, the desired estimates are direct consequences of Theorems 8.6 and 8.13. ∎

9. Blow up on the Cauchy horizon: Proof of Theorem 5.4

The goal of this subsection is to prove Theorem 5.4. We will first briefly describe the main ideas of the proof in Section 9.1. In Section 9.2, we will describe the notations and the setup of the proof. The three main types of L2L^{2} estimates, namely the almost energy conservation, the integrated local energy decay and the red-shift estimates, are proven in Sections 9.3, 9.4 and 9.5 respectively. In Section 9.6, we then put together all the estimates to prove the blow up statement (5.16). Finally, in Section 9.7, we use the blow up (5.16) to derive the blow up (5.17).

9.1. Idea of the proof

We prove (5.16) in Theorem 5.4 by showing its contrapositive, namely, we assume that (5.16) fails for some u<usu<u_{s} and deduce that the condition (5.15) must also fail on the event horizon. (Once (5.16) is proved, (5.17) follows straightforwardly - see Section 9.7.) The main idea behind the proof is to view the nonlinear unknown spacetime as a perturbation of Reissner--Nordström and to apply the argument6565 65 Recall that the proof Theorem 1.7 consists of an argument in the interior of the black hole region and an argument in the exterior of the black hole region. More precisely, we apply here the argument in [38] relevant to the interior region: see point (1) in the paragraph after the statement of Theorem 1.7. in the proof of Theorem 1.7. Here, we in particular use the bounds we obtained in the previous section to show that the spacetime in question is indeed close to Reissner–Nordström in an appropriate sense.

We quickly recall here our argument in [38] for proving Theorem 1.7. The main idea is to recast this as a decay problem. More precisely, we show that if (the linear analogue of) the conclusion of Theorem 5.4 is assumed to be false for some uu, then we can solve the wave equation towards i+i^{+} starting from the black hole interior and prove a strong enough decay bound on the event horizon which contradicts (the linear analogue of) the assumption of Theorem 5.4. Here, a key observation is that the original “blue-shift” effect from the point of view of the forward problem (which is the source of the instability at the first place) becomes a “red-shift” effect when the wave equation is solved in this direction. We then combine the following three types of L2L^{2} estimates: (1) an energy identity, (2) an integrated local energy decay estimate and (3) the red-shift estimates near both horizons to show the desired decay bounds on the event horizon.

On the other hand, for each of the above estimates, one faces the following challenges in applying the argument in [38] to the nonlinear setting at hand:

  1. (1)

    (Almost energy conservation) Unlike in [38], an exact conservation law does not hold in our setting. Instead, we only have an “almost conservation law” with error terms that decays according to the stability results proved in the previous section. In particular, in order to close the estimate for the almost energy conservation law, we must couple it with both the integrated local energy decay estimate and the red-shift estimates.

  2. (2)

    (Integrated local energy decay estimate) Unlike in exact Reissner–Nordström, in our setting λ\lambda and ν\nu cannot be controlled by Ω2\Omega^{2}. Instead, the differences λ−λR​N\lambda-\lambda_{RN} and ν−νR​N\nu-\nu_{RN} only decay polynomially in either |u||u| or vv. To deal with this, we in particular use a stronger integrated local energy decay estimate with a weight which is not smooth at the event horizon and the Cauchy horizon.6666 66 This estimate is reminiscent of the “irregular red-shift vector field” of Dafermos-Rodnianski [20].

  3. (3)

    (Red-shift estimates) Moreover, in the proof of the “red-shift” estimates near the Cauchy horizon (Proposition 9.4), the weaker bounds that we have for λ\lambda compared to the Reissner–Nordström case give much less room for the argument. Here, it is crucial that we have obtained the improved estimate in Proposition 8.15. (It is also for this estimate that we need to impose the condition α0<4​s−2\alpha_{0}<4s-2.)

9.3. Almost conserved energy

We begin with an “almost conserved energy” in the direction of i+i^{+}. To derive this, we notice that solutions to the linear wave equation on the Reissner--Nordström spacetime obeys a conservation law and show that in the coupled setting, the deviation from exact Reissner--Nordström can be controlled.6767 67 In the coupled setting, there is also a conservation law associated to the renormalized Hawking mass. We do not apply this in our setting in particular because the renormalized Hawking mass may be infinite at the Cauchy horizon (see Remark 1.10).

9.4. Integrated local energy decay estimate

Using the energy inequality, we now establish an integrated local energy decay estimate.

9.5. Red-shift estimates

In the next proposition, we prove an estimate that is localized near the Cauchy horizon. Since we are solving the wave equation “backwards” near the Cauchy horizon, the blue-shift effect becomes a red-shift effect as we approach i+i^{+}. This estimate in particular gives a good bulk term near the Cauchy horizon which has a better weight than that in (9.7).

Combining all these estimates and dropping the term (9.22) which has a good sign, we obtain the desired conclusion. ∎

Our next proposition is an analogue of Proposition 9.4, but instead localized near the event horizon. In particular, we have a good bulk term for ∂uϕ\partial_{u}\phi in this region which has a better weight compared to that in (9.7).

10. Stability and blow up on the entire Cauchy horizon: Proof of Theorem 5.5

In this section, we prove Theorem 5.5. Unlike Theorems 5.1 and 5.4, we need to work in the nonperturbative region, i.e., the spacetime is not necessarily close to a Reissner–Nordström in any quantitative sense. Special features of Einstein–Maxwell–(real)–scalar–field system in spherical symmetry therefore play an important role in the proof. A key step is propagation of L1L^{1}-type bounds on the metric coefficients and ϕ\phi, which hold initially thanks to Theorem 5.1, in characteristic rectangles with a lower bound on rr (Lemma 10.3). This strengthens the estimates for the scalar field in [14, Section 13].

We first introduce the coordinates (u,V)(u,V), which will be fixed for the remainder of this section. Fix an incoming null curve C¯1\underline{C}_{1} (maximally extended) whose past endpoint intersects ℋ1+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}. We define the coordinates (U,v)(U,v) by the gauge condition (5.11) on ℋ1+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1} and (5.13) (i.e., ∂Ur=−1\partial_{U}r=-1) on the whole C¯1\underline{C}_{1}, so that C¯1={(U,v):v=1}\underline{C}_{1}=\{(U,v):v=1\}. In particular, if we use the same initial incoming curve C¯1\underline{C}_{1}, then this coordinate system extends that of Theorem 5.1 past the perturbative region U≤UsU\leq U_{s}. As before, we define (u,V)(u,V) from (U,v)(U,v) by (5.8) and (5.10), respectively.

We record a basic observation regarding the coordinates (u,V)(u,V) on 𝒞​ℋ1+\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}.

Lemma 10.1.

After extending VV continuously to 𝒬+\mathcal{Q}^{+} with respect to the topology of ℝ1+1\mathbb{R}^{1+1}, the Cauchy horizon 𝒞​ℋ1+\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1} coincides with the curve {V=1}\{V=1\}. Moreover, uu is finite and nondegenerate (i.e., d​u≠0du\neq 0) on 𝒞​ℋ1+\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1} minus (possibly) the future endpoint. In particular, u𝒞​ℋ1+∈(−∞,∞]u_{\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}\in(-\infty,\infty] in the statement of Theorem 5.5 is well-defined.

Proof.

Fix an outgoing curve C∗C_{\ast} in 𝒬+\mathcal{Q}^{+} which intersects 𝒞​ℋ1+\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1} minus the future endpoint. Since 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is globally hyperbolic, C∗C_{\ast} intersects the initial hypersurface ℋ1+∪Σ∪ℋ2+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}\cup\Sigma\cup\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2}, from which it follows that C∗C_{\ast} intersects C¯1\underline{C}_{1} in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. Since the uu coordinate is constant on C∗C_{\ast}, it now suffices to verify that uu is finite and nondegenerate on every point in C¯1⊂𝒬\underline{C}_{1}\subset\mathcal{Q}.

By the condition (5.13), the Raychaudhuri equation (which ensures that rr decreases along C¯1\underline{C}_{1} in the incoming direction) and the fact that r≥0r\geq 0 on 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, the function UU is finite and nondegenerate on every point on C¯1∩𝒬\underline{C}_{1}\cap\mathcal{Q}. Since the change of variables (5.8) is nondegenerate and keeps u⁡(U)u(U) finite as long as UU is, the same statement holds for uu as desired. ∎

Consider a characteristic rectangle ℛ={(u,V):u1≤u≤u2,V1≤V<1}\mathcal{R}=\{(u,V):u_{1}\leq u\leq u_{2},\ V_{1}\leq V<1\}, where u1,u2,V1u_{1},u_{2},V_{1} are any numbers such that −∞<u1<u2<u𝒞​ℋ1+-\infty<u_{1}<u_{2}<u_{\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}} and V1>V⁡(1)V_{1}>V(1) (see Figure 8).

11. C2C^{2} inextendibility: Proof of Theorem 5.7

In this section, we prove the C2C^{2}-future-inextendibility of the maximal globally hyperbolic future development of the admissible Cauchy data satisfying the assumptions of Theorem 5.7. The proof will be based on a contradiction argument. We assume for the sake of argument that (ℳ,g)(\mathcal{M},g) as in Theorem 5.7 is future-extendible in C2C^{2}, i.e., we assume that there exist ι\iota and (ℳ~,g~)(\widetilde{\mathcal{M}},\tilde{g}) as in Definition 3.12. Our goal will be to derive a contradiction to the blow up of 1Ω2​∂Vϕ\frac{1}{\Omega^{2}}{\partial_{V}\phi} derived in Section 10.

In order to lighten the notation, let us write ι⁡(ℳ)\iota(\mathcal{M}) simply as ℳ\mathcal{M} when there is no danger of confusion. Given (ℳ,g)(\mathcal{M},g), (ℳ~,g~)(\widetilde{\mathcal{M}},\tilde{g}) and ι\iota as above, we will also denote by ∂ℳ\partial\mathcal{M} the (topological) boundary of ι⁡(ℳ)\iota(\mathcal{M}) in ℳ~\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}.

Let us briefly describe the ideas of the proof of Theorem 5.7. The proof consists of two main steps:

  1. (1)

    In the first part of the proof, using ideas in [35, 17], we will reduce the problem to ruling out radial null geodesics γ\gamma that exit ℳ\mathcal{M} through7474 74 Strictly speaking, it is the projection 𝝅⁡(γ)\boldsymbol{\pi}(\gamma) that exists through 𝒞​ℋ1+\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1} or 𝒞​ℋ2+\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2}, i.e., the closure of 𝝅⁡(γ)\boldsymbol{\pi}(\gamma) in 𝒬+\mathcal{Q}^{+} intersects 𝒞​ℋ1+\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1} or 𝒞​ℋ2+\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2}. 𝒞​ℋ1+\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1} or 𝒞​ℋ2+\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2} and entering ℳ~\widetilde{\mathcal{M}} and such that r>0r>0 at γ∩∂ℳ\gamma\cap\partial\mathcal{M}. (Lemmas 11.1-11.6 and Steps 1 and 2 in Lemma 11.7)

  2. (2)

    Next, suppose a radial null geodesic γ\gamma exits 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, say7575 75 The case where 𝒞​ℋ1+\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1} is replaced by 𝒞​ℋ2+\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2} is of course completely analogous., through 𝒞​ℋ1+\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}. We note that (5.18) implies that the Ricci curvature of a parallely propagated vector field blows up along γ\gamma. This clearly contradicts that γ\gamma is a geodesic in ℳ~\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}. (Step 3 in Lemma 11.7)

We now begin the first step of the proof with a standard result:

Lemma 11.1.

The boundary ∂ℳ\partial\mathcal{M} is locally an achronal Lipschitz hypersurface.

Proof.

This is standard and can be found for instance in [28]. ∎

The next lemma is due to Dafermos–Rendall [17]:

Lemma 11.2.

Proof.

The fact that any Killing vector field in (ℳ,g)(\mathcal{M},g) extends continuously to the boundary in the C2C^{2} extension (ℳ~,g~)(\widetilde{\mathcal{M}},\tilde{g}) is proven in [17]. The lemma thus follows as 𝒪1,𝒪2,𝒪3\mathcal{O}_{1},\mathcal{O}_{2},\mathcal{O}_{3} are Killing vector fields in (ℳ,g)(\mathcal{M},g). ∎

In particular, this implies,

This follows from Lemma 11.2 together with r2=12​∑i=13g⁡(𝒪i,𝒪i)r^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{3}g(\mathcal{O}_{i},\mathcal{O}_{i}). ∎

Equipped with Lemma 11.5, it now remains to show that both alternatives (1) and (2) cannot hold. The following lemma is immediate from results in [35].

Lemma 11.6.

Proof.

Lemma 11.7.

Proof.

Appendix A Subextremality of the event horizons

The goal of this section of the appendix is to prove Proposition 4.3. In what follows, we denote by (ℳ,g,ϕ,F)(\mathcal{M},g,\phi,F) a maximal globally hyperbolic future development of an ω0\omega_{0}-admissible initial data (where ω0>2\omega_{0}>2). First, we will need two lemmas, which will also be useful in later parts of the paper.

Lemma A.1 (The exterior regions are free of trapped (or anti-trapped) surfaces).
8080 80 A 22-sphere given by constant (u,v)(u,v) is called trapped (resp. anti-trapped) if ∂vr\partial_{v}r and ∂ur\partial_{u}r are both negative (resp. positive).

Let (u,v)(u,v) be a double null coordinate system on 𝒬=ℳ/S​O​(3)\mathcal{Q}=\mathcal{M}/SO(3) normalized according to Lemma 2.3. If u≤uℋ1+u\leq u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}, then

∂vr⁡(u,v)≥0,∂ur⁡(u,v)<0.\partial_{v}r(u,v)\geq 0,\quad\partial_{u}r(u,v)<0. (A.1)

If v≤vℋ2+v\leq v_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2}}, then

∂ur⁡(u,v)≥0,∂vr⁡(u,v)<0.\partial_{u}r(u,v)\geq 0,\quad\partial_{v}r(u,v)<0. (A.2)
Proof.

It clearly suffices to check (A.1) as (A.2) is similar. Suppose u≤uℋ1+u\leq u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}. We first establish ∂vr⁡(u,v)≥0\partial_{v}r(u,v)\geq 0. Assume this is not the case, i.e., there exists (uc,vc)∈𝒬(u_{c},v_{c})\in\mathcal{Q} with uc≤uℋ+u_{c}\leq u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}} such that ∂vr⁡(uc,vc)<0\partial_{v}r(u_{c},v_{c})<0. Then by continuity, there exists (uc′,vc′)∈𝒬(u_{c}^{\prime},v_{c}^{\prime})\in\mathcal{Q} such that uc′<uc≤uℋ+u_{c}^{\prime}<u_{c}\leq u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}} and ∂vr⁡(uc′,vc′)<0\partial_{v}r(u^{\prime}_{c},v^{\prime}_{c})<0. By the Raychaudhuri equation (2.4), we then have ∂vr⁡(uc′,v)<0\partial_{v}r(u^{\prime}_{c},v)<0 for every v≥vc′v\geq v^{\prime}_{c}, which contradicts the fact that supr⁡(uc′,⋅)=∞\sup r(u^{\prime}_{c},\cdot)=\infty (see Definition 4.2). Hence, we have established

∂vr⁡(u,v)≥0for ​u≤uℋ+.\partial_{v}r(u,v)\geq 0\quad\mbox{for }u\leq u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}}. (A.3)

Next, by the admissibility condition (3.4) (which by Lemma 2.3 implies ∂ur↾Σ0<0\partial_{u}r\restriction_{\Sigma_{0}}<0 for ρ≥ρ1\rho\geq\rho_{1} and ∂vr↾Σ0<0\partial_{v}r\restriction_{\Sigma_{0}}<0 for ρ≤ρ2\rho\leq\rho_{2}) and the Raychaudhuri equation (2.4), for every (u,v)∈𝒬(u,v)\in\mathcal{Q}, either ∂ur⁡(u,v)<0\partial_{u}r(u,v)<0 or ∂vr⁡(u,v)<0\partial_{v}r(u,v)<0. Hence, (A.1) follows from this observation and (A.3). ∎

Lemma A.2 (Limiting values of rr and ϖ\varpi on ℋ1+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1} and ℋ2+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2}).

Let (u,v)(u,v) be a double null coordinate system on 𝒬\mathcal{Q} normalized according to Lemma 2.3. Define

rℋ1+=supℋ1+r,rℋ2+=supℋ2+r,ϖℋ1+=supℋ1+ϖ,ϖℋ2+=supℋ2+ϖ.r_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}=\sup_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}r,\quad r_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2}}=\sup_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2}}r,\quad\varpi_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}=\sup_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}\varpi,\quad\varpi_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2}}=\sup_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2}}\varpi.

Then

rℋ1+=limv→∞r⁡(uℋ1+,v),rℋ2+=limu→∞r⁡(u,vℋ2+),ϖℋ1+=limv→∞ϖ⁡(uℋ1+,v),ϖℋ2+=limu→∞ϖ⁡(u,vℋ2+).r_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}=\lim_{v\to\infty}r(u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}},v),\quad r_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2}}=\lim_{u\to\infty}r(u,v_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2}}),\quad\varpi_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}=\lim_{v\to\infty}\varpi(u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}},v),\quad\varpi_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2}}=\lim_{u\to\infty}\varpi(u,v_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2}}). (A.4)

Moreover,

rℋ1+=ϖℋ1++ϖℋ1+2−𝐞2,rℋ2+=ϖℋ2++ϖℋ2+2−𝐞2.r_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}=\varpi_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}+\sqrt{\varpi_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}^{2}-{\bf e}^{2}},\quad r_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2}}=\varpi_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2}}+\sqrt{\varpi_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2}}^{2}-{\bf e}^{2}}. (A.5)
Proof.

In the proof, we only consider the case of ℋ1+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}; the other case can be handled similarly. We recall the (nontrivial!) fact that rℋ1+<∞r_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}<\infty. This follows from the Penrose inequality in the spherically symmetric setting, see [13, Lemma 3].

Step 1: Proof of (A.4). To prove (A.4) for rr, note that by Lemma 80, rr is non-decreasing (towards the future) along the event horizons. To prove (A.4) for ϖ\varpi, note that by Lemma 80 and the equations for ϖ\varpi in (2.8), ϖ\varpi is non-decreasing (towards the future) along the event horizons.

Step 2: Proof of rℋ1+=ϖℋ1+±ϖℋ1+2−𝐞2r_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}=\varpi_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}\pm\sqrt{\varpi_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}^{2}-{\bf e}^{2}}. Recall that 1−μ=−4Ω−2∂ur∂vr1-\mu=-4\Omega^{-2}\partial_{u}r\partial_{v}r. Thus by Lemma 80, we have 1−μ≥01-\mu\geq 0 in the exterior region {u≤uℋ1+}\{u\leq u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}\}. On ℋ1+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}, we claim that

lim infv→∞(1−μ)​(uℋ1+,v)=rℋ1+2−2​ϖℋ1+​rℋ1++𝐞2rℋ1+2=0.\liminf_{v\to\infty}(1-\mu)(u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}},v)=\frac{r_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}^{2}-2\varpi_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}r_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}+{\bf e}^{2}}{r_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}^{2}}=0. (A.6)

Since 0<r↾Σ0∩ℋ1+≤rℋ1+<∞0<r\restriction_{\Sigma_{0}\cap\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}\leq r_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}<\infty, the desired formula for rℋ1+r_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}} would then follow by the quadratic formula.

For the purpose of contradiction, suppose that (A.6) is false. Hence there exists c>0c>0 and v0v_{0} such that

(1−μ)​(uℋ1+,v)≥c for ​v≥v0.(1-\mu)(u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}},v)\geq c\quad\hbox{ for }v\geq v_{0}. (A.7)

The idea is to show that (A.7), when combined with the fact that rℋ1+<∞r_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}<\infty, implies that rr is also bounded on nearby outgoing null curves, which contradicts Definition 4.2.

To make this idea precise, we use a bootstrap argument. Let ε>0\varepsilon>0 and A≥2A\geq 2 be small and large parameters (respectively) to be fixed later. Replacing v0v_{0} by a larger number if necessary, we may ensure that rℋ1+−r⁡(uℋ1+,v0)<εr_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}-r(u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}},v_{0})<\varepsilon and ϖℋ1+−ϖ⁡(uℋ1+,v0)<ε\varpi_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}-\varpi(u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}},v_{0})<\varepsilon. Furthermore, we choose u0<uℋ1+u_{0}<u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}} so that r⁡(u0,v0)−r⁡(uℋ1+,v0)<εr(u_{0},v_{0})-r(u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}},v_{0})<\varepsilon and ϖ⁡(u0,v0)−ϖ⁡(uℋ1+,v0)<ε\varpi(u_{0},v_{0})-\varpi(u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}},v_{0})<\varepsilon. Given v1>v0v_{1}>v_{0}, we make the bootstrap assumption

r⁡(u0,v)−r⁡(uℋ1+,v)<4​ε,ϖ⁡(u0,v)−ϖ⁡(uℋ1+,v)<2​A​ε for ​v0≤v≤v1,r(u_{0},v)-r(u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}},v)<4\varepsilon,\quad\varpi(u_{0},v)-\varpi(u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}},v)<2A\varepsilon\quad\hbox{ for }v_{0}\leq v\leq v_{1}, (A.8)

which initially holds for some v1>v0v_{1}>v_{0} by continuity. For a large enough AA and a sufficiently small ε\varepsilon, we claim that (A.8) can be improved to

r⁡(u0,v)−r⁡(uℋ1+,v)<2​ε,ϖ⁡(u0,v)−ϖ⁡(uℋ1+,v)<A​ε for ​v0≤v≤v1.r(u_{0},v)-r(u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}},v)<2\varepsilon,\quad\varpi(u_{0},v)-\varpi(u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}},v)<A\varepsilon\quad\hbox{ for }v_{0}\leq v\leq v_{1}. (A.9)

From the claim, it would follow (via a simple continuity argument) that r⁡(u0,v)−r⁡(uℋ1+,v)<2​εr(u_{0},v)-r(u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}},v)<2\varepsilon for every v≥v1v\geq v_{1}, which is impossible due to Definition 4.2 and the fact that rℋ1+<∞r_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}<\infty.

By (A.7) and the bootstrap assumption (A.8), we have

(1−μ)​(u,v)≥c2 for ​(u,v)∈[u0,uℋ1+]×[v0,v1](1-\mu)(u,v)\geq\frac{c}{2}\quad\hbox{ for }(u,v)\in[u_{0},u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}]\times[v_{0},v_{1}]

for a small enough ε\varepsilon (depending only on cc and AA). By the first equation in (2.8), it follows that

in [u0,uℋ1+]×[v0,v1][u_{0},u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}]\times[v_{0},v_{1}]. Integrating in vv, we see that e−C​ε≤−∂ur(u,v)−∂ur(u,v0)≤eC​εe^{-C\varepsilon}\leq\frac{-\partial_{u}r(u,v)}{-\partial_{u}r(u,v_{0})}\leq e^{C\varepsilon}. Hence, for sufficiently small ε\varepsilon, the first inequality of (A.9) follows.

To improve the estimate for ϖ\varpi (i.e., the second inequality of (A.9)), we need to use the other equations in (2.8). Let (u,v)∈[u0,uℋ1+]×[v0,v1](u,v)\in[u_{0},u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}]\times[v_{0},v_{1}]. By the first and the second equations, as well as the preceding estimates, we have

∫v0v|∂vϕ|(u,v′)​d​v′≤\displaystyle\int_{v_{0}}^{v}|\partial_{v}\phi|(u,v^{\prime})\,dv^{\prime}\leq (∫v0v12​r2​(1−μ)​(∂vϕ)2∂vr​(u,v′)​d​v′)1/2​(∫v0v2r2​(1−μ)​∂vr⁡(u,v′)​d​v′)1/2\displaystyle\left(\int_{v_{0}}^{v}\frac{1}{2}r^{2}(1-\mu)\frac{(\partial_{v}\phi)^{2}}{\partial_{v}r}(u,v^{\prime})\,dv^{\prime}\right)^{1/2}\left(\int_{v_{0}}^{v}\frac{2}{r^{2}(1-\mu)}\partial_{v}r(u,v^{\prime})\,dv^{\prime}\right)^{1/2}
≤\displaystyle\leq C​(ϖ⁡(u,v)−ϖ⁡(u,v0))1/2​(r⁡(u,v)−r⁡(u,v0))1/2≤C​ε.\displaystyle C(\varpi(u,v)-\varpi(u,v_{0}))^{1/2}(r(u,v)-r(u,v_{0}))^{1/2}\leq C\varepsilon.

in [u0,uℋ1+]×[v0,v1][u_{0},u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}]\times[v_{0},v_{1}]. Integrating in uu and using the bootstrap assumption, we obtain

Step 3: Proof of (A.5). Since rℋ1+>0r_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}>0, we necessarily have ϖℋ1+>0\varpi_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}>0 by the previous step. When ϖℋ1+=|𝐞|\varpi_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}=|{\bf e}|, which corresponds to the extremal case, there is nothing to prove. Therefore, we may assume that |𝐞|<ϖℋ1+|{\bf e}|<\varpi_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}} and moreover focus on ruling out the scenario rℋ1+=ϖℋ1+−ϖℋ1+2−𝐞2r_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}=\varpi_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}-\sqrt{\varpi_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}^{2}-{\bf e}^{2}}.

By the monotonicity properties of ϖ\varpi in the exterior region u≤uℋ1+u\leq u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}} (using Lemma 80), we can find vf​a​rv_{far} such that ϖ⁡(u,v)>|𝐞|\varpi(u,v)>|{\bf e}| in the characteristic rectangle ℛ={u≤uℋ1+,v≥vf​a​r}\mathcal{R}=\{u\leq u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}},\ v\geq v_{far}\}. Recall from Step 2 that

1−μ=r2−2​ϖ​r+𝐞2r2≥0​ where ​u≤uℋ1+.1-\mu=\frac{r^{2}-2\varpi r+{\bf e}^{2}}{r^{2}}\geq 0\hbox{ where }u\leq u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}.

Since rℋ1+=ϖℋ1+−ϖℋ1+2−𝐞2r_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}=\varpi_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}-\sqrt{\varpi_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}^{2}-{\bf e}^{2}}, it follows (by a continuity argument) that r⁡(u,v)≤ϖ⁡(u,v)−ϖ2​(u,v)−𝐞2r(u,v)\leq\varpi(u,v)-\sqrt{\varpi^{2}(u,v)-{\bf e}^{2}} in ℛ\mathcal{R}. In particular, r≤supΣ0∩{u≤uℋ1+}ϖ<∞r\leq\sup_{\Sigma_{0}\cap\{u\leq u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}}\}}\varpi<\infty in ℛ\mathcal{R}, which is impossible in view of Definition 4.2. ∎

We are now ready to prove Proposition 4.3:

Proof of Proposition 4.3.

Define double null coordinates according to Lemma 2.3. Define u¯​(v)\underline{u}(v) and v¯​(u)\underline{v}(u) such that (u,v¯​(u)),(u¯​(v),v)∈Σ0(u,\underline{v}(u)),\,(\underline{u}(v),v)\in\Sigma_{0}. We prove the proposition only for ℋ1+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1} as the proof for ℋ2+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{2} is similar. For the rest of this proof, ℋ1+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1} will be denoted as ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+}. Moreover, let uℋ+=uℋ1+u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}}=u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1}} be defined as in Definition 4.2. Without loss of generality, we assume that 𝐞>0{\bf e}>0.

Step 0: Limit must be subextremal or extremal. Let us first note that the limit along ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+} must be either subextremal (limv→∞ϖ⁡(uℋ+,v)>𝐞\lim_{v\to\infty}\varpi(u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}},v)>{\bf e}) or extremal (limv→∞ϖ⁡(uℋ+,v)=𝐞\lim_{v\to\infty}\varpi(u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}},v)={\bf e}). This follows from (A.5) and the fact that rℋ+r_{\mathcal{H}^{+}} is real.

Contradiction assumption: Suppose for the sake of contradiction that the limit along ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+} is extremal, i.e., limv→∞ϖ⁡(uℋ+,v)=𝐞\lim_{v\to\infty}\varpi(u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}},v)={\bf e}.

Step 1: Definition of u∗u_{*}, u∗⁣∗u_{**} and v∗v_{*}. Let

v∗=inf{v∈ℝ:∂vr⁡(u¯​(v′),v′)≥0​ for all ​v′≥v}.v_{*}=\inf\{v\in\mathbb{R}:\partial_{v}r(\underline{u}(v^{\prime}),v^{\prime})\geq 0\mbox{ for all }v^{\prime}\geq v\}.

Such a v∗v_{*} exists since the set above is non-empty and bounded below, by the asymptotic flatness condition (3.1) and Lemma 2.3. Moreover,

  1. (1)

    it holds that v∗≤v¯​(uℋ+)v_{*}\leq\underline{v}(u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}}) by Lemma 80; and

  2. (2)

    it also holds that there exists an ϵc>0\epsilon_{c}>0 such that ∂ur⁡(u,v¯​(u))<0\partial_{u}r(u,\underline{v}(u))<0 for all u∈(−∞,u¯​(v∗)+ϵc)u\in(-\infty,\underline{u}(v_{*})+\epsilon_{c}) by the admissibility condition (3.4).

Notice in particular that by the continuity of ∂vr\partial_{v}r, we have ∂vr⁡(u¯​(v∗),v∗)=0\partial_{v}r(\underline{u}(v_{*}),v_{*})=0.

Next, choose u∗>u¯​(v∗)u_{*}>\underline{u}(v_{*}) such that ∂vr⁡(u∗,v¯​(u∗))<0\partial_{v}r(u_{*},\underline{v}(u_{*}))<0. By the definition of v∗v_{*}, u∗>u¯​(v∗)u_{*}>\underline{u}(v_{*}) can be chosen arbitrarily close to u¯​(v∗)\underline{u}(v_{*}) such that

  1. (1)

    the region 𝒟∗={(u,v):u∈[u¯(v∗),u∗],v∈[v¯(u),v∗]}\mathcal{D}_{*}=\{(u,v):u\in[\underline{u}(v_{*}),u_{*}],\,v\in[\underline{v}(u),v_{*}]\} is contained in the maximal globally hyperbolic future development of the initial data; and

  2. (2)

    ∂ur⁡(u,v¯​(u))<0\partial_{u}r(u,\underline{v}(u))<0 for all u≤u∗u\leq u_{*} (for which we use point (2) in the properties of v∗v_{*} above).

By the Raychaudhuri equation (2.4), it follows that

∂ur⁡(u,v)<0 for all ​(u,v)∈𝒟∗.\partial_{u}r(u,v)<0\quad\hbox{ for all }(u,v)\in\mathcal{D}_{\ast}. (A.10)

Now on the constant v=v∗v=v_{*} curve, define u∗⁣∗u_{**} by

u∗⁣∗=sup{u≥u¯​(v∗):∂vr⁡(u′,v∗)≥0​ for all ​u′∈[u¯​(v∗),u]}.u_{**}=\sup\{u\geq\underline{u}(v_{*}):\partial_{v}r(u^{\prime},v_{*})\geq 0\mbox{ for all }u^{\prime}\in[\underline{u}(v_{*}),u]\}.

Such an u∗⁣∗≥u¯​(v∗)u_{**}\geq\underline{u}(v_{*}) exists since the set is nonempty (by the fact ∂vr⁡(u¯​(v∗),v∗)=0\partial_{v}r(\underline{u}(v_{*}),v_{*})=0) and bounded above (since ∂vr⁡(u∗,v∗)<0\partial_{v}r(u_{*},v_{*})<0 by the choice of u∗u_{*} and the Raychaudhuri equation (2.4)).

The points defined above are depicted in the diagram below:

Step 2: Monotonicity of ϖ\varpi and rr. We now connect ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+} to the point (u∗⁣∗,v∗)(u_{**},v_{*}) via a piecewise smooth curve γ\gamma with increasing uu and decreasing vv as depicted in Figure 9. More precisely, we connect γ⁡(0)=(uℋ+,v¯​(uℋ+))\gamma(0)=(u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}},\underline{v}(u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}})) to γ⁡(12)=(u¯​(v∗),v∗)\gamma(\frac{1}{2})=(\underline{u}(v_{*}),v_{*}) following Σ0\Sigma_{0}, then connect γ⁡(12)\gamma(\frac{1}{2}) to γ⁡(1)=(u∗⁣∗,v∗)\gamma(1)=(u_{**},v_{*}) following the null curve {v=v∗}\{v=v_{*}\}.

While it is possible that γ\gamma is degenerate (i.e., constant in the parameter) in some parts, we nevertheless have γ˙u≥0\dot{\gamma}^{u}\geq 0 and γ˙v≤0\dot{\gamma}^{v}\leq 0. Moreover, by the construction in Step 1, we have ∂ur<0\partial_{u}r<0 and ∂vr≥0\partial_{v}r\geq 0 on the image of γ\gamma. Therefore, dd​s​r∘γ⁡(s)=γ˙u​∂ur+γ˙v​∂vr≤0\frac{d}{ds}r\circ\gamma(s)=\dot{\gamma}^{u}\partial_{u}r+\dot{\gamma}^{v}\partial_{v}r\leq 0 and dd​s​ϖ∘γ⁡(s)=γ˙u​∂uϖ+γ˙v​∂vϖ≤0\frac{d}{ds}\varpi\circ\gamma(s)=\dot{\gamma}^{u}\partial_{u}\varpi+\dot{\gamma}^{v}\partial_{v}\varpi\leq 0 (where we used (2.8)). It follows that

ϖ⁡(u∗⁣∗,v∗)≤\displaystyle\varpi(u_{**},v_{*})\leq ϖ⁡(uℋ+,v¯​(uℋ+))≤limv→∞ϖ⁡(uℋ+,v)=𝐞,\displaystyle\varpi(u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}},\underline{v}(u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}}))\leq\lim_{v\to\infty}\varpi(u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}},v)={\bf e}, (A.11)
r⁡(u∗⁣∗,v∗)≤\displaystyle r(u_{**},v_{*})\leq r⁡(uℋ+,v¯​(uℋ+))≤limv→∞r⁡(uℋ+,v)=𝐞.\displaystyle r(u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}},\underline{v}(u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}}))\leq\lim_{v\to\infty}r(u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}},v)={\bf e}. (A.12)

Step 3: Conclusion of the proof. By the first equation in (2.8) and the definition of μ\mu, we have

∂u∂vr⁡(u∗⁣∗,v∗)=−Ω2​(ϖ−𝐞2r)2​r2​(u∗⁣∗,v∗)≥0,\partial_{u}\partial_{v}r(u_{**},v_{*})=-\frac{\Omega^{2}(\varpi-\frac{{\bf e}^{2}}{r})}{2r^{2}}(u_{**},v_{*})\geq 0, (A.13)

where the last inequality follows from (A.11) and (A.12). On the other hand, it is impossible to have ∂u∂vr⁡(u∗⁣∗,v∗)>0\partial_{u}\partial_{v}r(u_{**},v_{*})>0. Indeed, this contradicts the choice of u∗⁣∗u_{**} as one would then have ∂vr⁡(u,v∗)≥0\partial_{v}r(u,v_{*})\geq 0 for uu in a neighborhood of u∗⁣∗u_{**}.

Therefore, in order to conclude the contradiction argument, it suffices to rule out ∂u∂vr⁡(u∗⁣∗,v∗)=0\partial_{u}\partial_{v}r(u_{**},v_{*})=0. In view of the above argument, this holds only if equalities hold in (A.11) and (A.12), i.e., ϖ⁡(u∗⁣∗,v∗)=r⁡(u∗⁣∗,v∗)=𝐞\varpi(u_{**},v_{*})=r(u_{**},v_{*})=\bf e. Now, by (A.10), ∂ur⁡(u∗⁣∗,v∗)<0\partial_{u}r(u_{**},v_{*})<0. Importantly, this is a strict inequality. Thus, there exist c>0c>0 and ϵr>0\epsilon_{r}>0 such that r⁡(u,v∗)−𝐞≤−𝐜⁡(𝐮−𝐮∗⁣∗)r(u,v_{*})-\bf e\leq-c(u-u_{**}) for u∈[u∗⁣∗,u∗⁣∗+ϵr]u\in[u_{**},u_{**}+\epsilon_{r}]. Using the fact that Ω2\Omega^{2}, ϖ\varpi and rr are C1C^{1} and also the monotonicity (A.11), one deduces that there exist c′>0c^{\prime}>0 and ϵr′>0\epsilon_{r}^{\prime}>0 such that

∂u∂vr⁡(u,v∗)≥c′​(u−u∗⁣∗)\partial_{u}\partial_{v}r(u,v_{*})\geq c^{\prime}(u-u_{**})

for u∈[u∗⁣∗,u∗⁣∗+ϵr′]u\in[u_{**},u_{**}+\epsilon^{\prime}_{r}]. This then contradicts the choice of u∗⁣∗u_{**} as ∂vr⁡(u,v∗)≥0\partial_{v}r(u,v_{*})\geq 0 for uu in a neighborhood of u∗⁣∗u_{**}. This concludes the contradiction argument. ∎

Appendix B Gauge condition on the event horizon

In the statement of Theorem 5.1, we imposed a gauge condition (5.11) on C−∞C_{-\infty} which is most convenient for proving the estimates. On the other hand, it is less convenient to apply the theorem with this gauge condition (and in fact it is a priori not entirely clear that such a gauge exists). In this section of the appendix, we compare the gauge condition (5.11) with the gauge condition ∂vr1−μ=1\frac{\partial_{v}r}{1-\mu}=1, which is more often used in the literature (for instance in [18]). Ω~ℋ2:=−2g(∂U,∂v~)=4​e−2​κ+​r+​(r+−r−)1+κ+κ−r+2e2​κ+​v~ on C−∞.\widetilde{\Omega}^{2}_{\mathcal{H}}:=-2g(\partial_{U},\partial_{\widetilde{v}})=\frac{4e^{-2\kappa_{+}r_{+}}(r_{+}-r_{-})^{1+\frac{\kappa_{+}}{\kappa_{-}}}}{r_{+}^{2}}e^{2\kappa_{+}\widetilde{v}}\quad\hbox{ on }C_{-\infty}. (B.1)

Proof.

It suffices to solve for a function v~​(v)\widetilde{v}(v) such that v~​(1)=1\widetilde{v}(1)=1, C−1≤d​v~d​v≤CC^{-1}\leq\frac{d\widetilde{v}}{dv}\leq C, where the constant C>0C>0 may depend on EE, ss, MM, 𝐞{\bf e}, r0r_{0} and ∂Ur⁡(0,1)\partial_{U}r(0,1), and

e−2​κ+​r+​(r+−r−)1+κ+κ−r+2e2​κ+​v~​(v)=−∂Ur(0,v)(d​v~d​v(v))−1.\frac{e^{-2\kappa_{+}r_{+}}(r_{+}-r_{-})^{1+\frac{\kappa_{+}}{\kappa_{-}}}}{r_{+}^{2}}e^{2\kappa_{+}\widetilde{v}(v)}=-\partial_{U}r(0,v)\left(\frac{d\widetilde{v}}{dv}(v)\right)^{-1}. (B.2)

Step 1: Estimating the decay of ∂vr\partial_{v}r. By (b) and (c), it follows that limv→+∞(1−μ)=0\lim_{v\to+\infty}(1-\mu)=0. Hence, using (a),

limv→+∞∂vr=0.\lim_{v\to+\infty}\partial_{v}r=0. (B.3)

We now want to get a quantitative decay estimate for ∂vr\partial_{v}r. Using the Raychaudhuri equations in (2.4), −Ω24​∂Ur=∂vr1−μ=1-\frac{\Omega^{2}}{4\partial_{U}r}=\frac{\partial_{v}r}{1-\mu}=1 (cf. (2.6)) and (2.8), we obtain

By the method of integrating factors, we have

(B.5)

By (B.3) and limv→∞2​(ϖ−𝐞2r)r2​(v)=2​κ+\lim_{v\to\infty}\frac{2(\varpi-\frac{{\bf e}^{2}}{r})}{r^{2}}(v)=2\kappa_{+}, where the latter follows from the conditions (b) and (c), it follows that the first term on the right-hand side vanishes.

To further analyze (B.5), we need some information regarding rr and ϖ\varpi. For rr, we note the preliminary lower and upper bounds r0≤r≤M+M2−𝐞2r_{0}\leq r\leq M+\sqrt{M^{2}-{\bf e}^{2}}. For ϖ\varpi, by (2.8), (c) and (d), we have

and as a consequence

|M+M2−𝐞2−r⁡(v)|≤C​v−2​s+1​ on ​J,|M+\sqrt{M^{2}-{\bf e}^{2}}-r(v)|\leq Cv^{-2s+1}\hbox{ on }J, (B.8)

where CC is independent of JJ.
